item.title: Worried You Might be Watching Too Much TV? 5 Things to Know
item.description:
Habit Formation

Worried You Might be Watching Too Much TV? 5 Things to Know

Is guilt after your second hour of TV needed, or needless?

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • A certain amount of online watching can offer a reset and other healthy benefits.
  • How you feel when you step away, and other signs, may signal it’s too much.
  • A few reflective questions can let you throw away the guilt and simply enjoy the pleasure… or not.
Source: eclipse_images/Getty Images Signature

“What is it about us as a culture that we have to put ‘guilty’ in front of ‘pleasure’?” -Alexis Soloski, New York Times culture reporter

I can’t even quantify how many women came into my office, back in the day, confessing guilt for binge-watching Gilmore Girls. Or Friends. Or whatever. Sometimes, they admitted watching it over and over again. We spent hours assessing if it was a problem (it usually wasn’t) and helping them feel okay—maybe even good—about this secret “habit.” Perhaps their newborn had just gotten released from the neonatal ICU, or a parent was sick, or their job was a burnout or their partner was cheating. Binging Gilmore Girls? What a healthy response! They could’ve been smoking or drinking in excess, or working on a revenge scenario to slash their partner’s tires or make off with their earnings for Bermuda.

There’s flak everywhere you look in our (historically Puritan-dominant) culture about screentime. And, of course, it’s true: we can get addicted (and surely are) to screens, as well as to drinks, substances, sex, or food. Having an unhealthy relationship with anyone or anything is bad for us.

But we know that. What we might not know is that some screen time can be healthy. Watching a favorite comedy after a long day or winding down with a beloved action or game show can help us regulate, recover, transition, and turn towards what’s next. Whether that’s making dinner, having patience with our kids or partner (or self!), or starting that second shift with the side hustle we’ve been working on, viewing TV first might offer renewed energy and a softened mood. And perhaps even a few more steps on that treadmill while we get to the end of an episode.

Actual research on watching or “binge”-watching is scant, but we do know a few things:

  • A “binge” means different things to different people. Is it one hour or six? Two episodes or five? It’s clear “too much” is not good, but that’s individual. Do you step away feeling worse or having ignored things you needed to do? Do you find yourself facing someone irritated that you’re watching “too much”? That may suggest a problem. Alternatively, do you stop watching and feel renewed and ready for what’s next? Whether you call that a binge or not, it may be your sweet spot.
  • Re-watching a show you love can be predictable and comforting. You know what will happen next, you’re not stressed out by worrying your favorite character will wind up in that assassin’s sights, you look forward to that scene where they finally reconcile… Knowing the plot is reassuring and soothing, like re-reading a favorite novel and knowing beloved characters thrive, yet again.
  • Speaking of characters, they can be almost like friends. Sure, they aren’t real and don’t replace needed social activity. You may not even think about them in a day or two. But watching others struggle, thrive, lose, or win is an emotional release at least as old as Greek theater. It helps us imagine and dream, and even process.
  • If you watch something with relationship themes and then discuss it with your partner, it could decrease your break-up or divorce risk! Talking about someone else’s relationship problems seems to take the sting out of discussing (or blaming) one another, making it easier to take another person’s perspective. That’s been found to increase empathy and help relationships survive.
  • Take a load off. Watching something on the tube or screen helps you let go of the barrage of stimuli built-up from the day (what we call cognitive fatigue) and reset your calm. Yes, we turn off, but in a good way. Like a nap for the brain. Meanwhile, if we choose something pleasurable (from rom-com to horror; docudrama to anime—there’s no judgment here!), we might even gain a good boost of dopamine.
article continues after advertisement

As with all things, motivation helps offer clues to the question of enough or too much. Do you turn to online entertainment to unwind or de-stress with more soothing narratives than your day provided? If so, and you step away within reason, screen- (or even a bit of binge-) watching can be rejuvenating. Toss that guilt and keep the pleasure! If you’re avoiding what you need to do or who you need to be with, or you can’t pull away (maybe feeling even darker if you do), remember help awaits, whenever you’re ready.

item.title: The Wednesday Effect
item.description:
Motivation

The Wednesday Effect

Why your most ordinary days matter the most.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Ordinary days are meaningful opportunities to start and form new habits.
  • Don’t wait for a fresh start; small actions today create change.
  • Make habits part of who you are, not just goals on a to-do list.
  • Choose consistency over perfection; imperfect progress still counts.

By Emily Balcetis and Flora Zik

It is an ordinary Wednesday evening. The clock reads 8:00 p.m. Nothing remarkable happened today, and nothing remarkable is waiting tomorrow. No milestone. No fresh start. No surge of motivation.

What do you do with the next hour?

Waiting for the “right” moment to change might actually just be procrastination.
Source: Brett Jordan/ Unsplash

We often imagine that change begins with a clean slate: January 1st, a new semester, or a major birthday. But life is rarely defined by those standout moments. It is shaped by ordinary Wednesday nights.

The choices you make when nothing feels urgent add up. They become routines, routines become habits, and over time those habits become part of your identity.

If you've ever wondered why ordinary days so often slip away without bringing you closer to your goals, psychology offers three surprising explanations—and practical ways to change course.

Explanation 1. You're Waiting for the Perfect Time to Start, but Don’t Need to

There is something comforting about a fresh start. We tell ourselves we'll start exercising after the holidays, open a savings account next month, or get organized when spring hits. We keep searching for the perfect moment to reinvent ourselves.

The problem is that waiting for the "right" time can become a form of procrastination.

Research supports this idea. In a 2019 study published in Current Opinion in Psychology, Hengchen Dai and Claire Li at the University of California, Los Angeles, found that when people anticipate a temporal landmark—such as an anniversary or starting a new job—they tend to see their future self as separate from their current self. As a result, they may optimistically believe that their future self will take responsibility for today's goals, making it easier to put them off.

If we keep waiting for a better time to change, we can spend far more time preparing than actually changing. The perfect moment rarely arrives.

Suggestion To Kickstart a Better Habit: Stop Waiting for a Fresh Start

Instead of asking yourself, "When can I do this perfectly?" ask, "What's the smallest version of this I can do today?" If it still feels overwhelming, make it smaller.

You don't need to study for three hours. Study for 20 minutes. If you don't have time for a full workout, take a 15-minute walk. Instead of trying to overhaul your entire routine, make one choice that moves you a little closer to the person you want to become.

If we wait until we feel motivated, we may not ever get started. Try instead to just begin. Small starts have a way of becoming lasting habits.

Explanation 2. You Don't See the Habit as Part of Who You Are

The stories you tell yourself shape your choices. If you keep thinking, "I'm terrible at sticking with things," skipping today's workout starts to feel consistent with who you are. It gives you a pass, when you don’t need or want one.

Some aspects of identity we are born into, but other aspects of identity are flexible and can be cultivated.

A 2025 review conducted by Kristie-Lee R. Alfrey, published in Behavioral Sciences Journal, examined dozens of studies on identity and behavior. Across actions as different as exercising, studying, and seeking support from others, one pattern emerged: People were more likely to consistently perform a behavior when they saw it as part of their identity. In other words, habits stick more easily when they feel like an expression of who you are rather than another item on your to-do list.

Suggestion To Kickstart a Better Habit: Focus on Who You're Becoming

Instead of saying what you are not, introduce yourself as who you will be in the future.

Swap "I can't run" for "I'm becoming a runner." Trade out "I'm broke" and replace it with "I'm working on saving for my future."

These rhetorical replacements may seem small, but each one is evidence of the identity you're building.

Explanation 3. You Think If You Can’t Do It Perfectly, You Shouldn’t Do It at All

Perfection isn’t the goal. Consistency means making choices that move you forward, even imperfectly.
Source: Alexas_fotos / Unsplash

Sometimes the biggest obstacle to consistency isn't procrastination—it's perfectionism. We set an ambitious goal and then treat anything short of it as failure.

Imagine you've decided to read 30 pages every night. By Wednesday, you're exhausted and it's already 10 p.m. You know you won't hit that goal, so you skip trying altogether.

Research by Jessica Höpfner at Technical University of Darmstadt, Germany, published in Frontiers, explains why this mindset is so common. Across two studies, people who were randomly assigned to fall short of a high, specific goal experienced drops in mood, self-esteem, and motivation. Those feelings also made them less likely to tackle future challenges. In other words, when we treat goals as all-or-nothing, falling short today can make us less likely to try again tomorrow.

This all-or-nothing thinking turns every ordinary day into a pass-or-fail test. Real life, of course, rarely works that way.

Suggestion To Kickstart a Better Habit: Trade Perfection for Consistency

Instead of asking, "Did I do everything I planned?" ask: "Did I do something that moved me forward?"

Saving $20 still counts. Two thousand steps still count. Reading two pages still counts. Progress doesn't stop counting just because it falls short of perfection.

The goal isn't to lower your standards. It's to recognize that imperfect progress is still progress. Often, the most productive thing you can do is refuse to let one imperfect day become the reason you stop altogether.

Your Life Is Mostly Made of Wednesdays

The everydays are when change can really happen.
Source: Iga Palacz / Unsplash

It is easy to underestimate a typical day because it does not feel important while you are living it.

You probably will not remember the Wednesday night when you went for a 20-minute walk. You probably will not remember replacing the slice of cake with a cup of fruit last week. Those small choices may not be memorable, but they can be meaningful. Over time, they become the routines that shape your life.

Let's go back to that Wednesday night at 8 p.m. It wasn't New Year's Day. It wasn't your birthday. It wasn't a magical moment when you suddenly felt more disciplined or motivated. It was just an ordinary Wednesday—and that's exactly why it matters.

Instead of waiting for the perfect day to become the person you want to be, ask yourself: What would that person do today? That's the question that kickstarts change.

Flora Zik is earning her Bachelor's Degree in Cognitive Science at The University of California, Los Angeles.

item.title: 2 Antidotes To Chronic "Relationship Overthinking"
item.description:
Relationships

2 Antidotes To Chronic "Relationship Overthinking"

If you replay your fights, breakdowns and breakups, this might be the reason.

Posted October 5, 2026

Many people arrive in therapy seeking answers to a relationship that has gone wrong. They say things like:

  • “We were so good in the beginning. What did I do to cause things to change?”
  • “I keep replaying our last conversation in my head. I still don’t know where it came from or how to respond.”
  • “I simply can’t get over the thought that this whole thing was somehow my fault.”

Searching for answers when a relationship is on the rocks, or has recently ended, is a normal response. However, excessive rumination, thought-spiraling and fixation can lead to deeper psychological issues. Although we all have a natural tendency to want to understand the sequence of events that caused the breakdown, we also owe it to ourselves to protect our mental health. This sometimes means avoiding trying to make sense of nuanced and inexplicable scenarios. It also means steering clear of self-blaming cycles.

Here is one way to know if you struggle with relationship overthinking, as well as two strategies to turn difficult episodes into opportunities for growth.

The Mistake Rumination Scale

Psychologists have designed various instruments to assess an individual’s tendency to become bogged down or “stuck” in destructive thought patterns, especially pertaining to one’s closest relationships. One such test is the Mistake Rumination Scale, authored by a team of researchers at the University of British Columbia and York University.

To gauge your propensity for getting stuck on things that have gone wrong, read through the following seven questions and ask yourself how often they apply to you.

  1. When you make a mistake, to what extent do you tend to think “How could I be so stupid?”
  2. When you make a mistake, to what extent do you tend to think “Why can’t I stop making mistakes like this?”
  3. When you make a mistake, to what extent do you tend to think about the mistake and wish it had gone better?
  4. When you make a mistake, to what extent do you tend to think “Why do I make mistakes that other people don’t make?”
  5. When you make a mistake, to what extent do you tend to think about other mistakes you have made?
  6. When you make a mistake, to what extent do you tend to think “Why couldn’t I have seen this coming and have found some way to avoid it?”
  7. When you make a mistake, to what extent do you tend to think “I am not going to let other people know about this?”

If you find yourself resonating with the questions above, it’s likely that you are especially sensitive to conflict and breakdowns in your close relationships. This is true of everyone, but you probably take it particularly hard. You may try to think your way out of relationship problems, which only adds gravity to the problem and weighs down your psyche.

Fortunately, there are many ways to keep your relationship overthinking habit at bay. Here are two possible solutions.

1. Flex Your Perspective-Taking Muscle

People who get caught up in a cycle of relationship rumination and overthinking can often benefit from a change in perspective. For instance, instead of thinking “how did I cause this problem to happen and how can I fix it?” try flipping the script to “what position or frame of mind was my partner in to cause them to act like this?” Taking the perspective of the other person can help you assess the situation as if you were an objective third party. Asking a friend or a therapist for their perspective on the matter can also help you see the problem from an outside lens.

article continues after advertisement

Remember, rumination is a self-directed journey through one’s thoughts and emotions, often leading to dead ends. To break the cycle, it’s important to adopt, and fully commit to, a new perspective.

2. Make a Radical Change

Sometimes, it’s our environment, routine and the people we surround ourselves with that keep us fixated on an unhelpful thought. One way to break out of a destructive thought pattern is, therefore, to make a radical change to your lifestyle. This could mean any number of things, such as:

  • Taking a break from social media
  • Seeking out the counsel of a qualified mental health professional
  • Committing to a new exercise routine
  • Taking a vacation
  • Finding a new job
  • Moving to a new town or city

It’s not guaranteed to work, but it’s worth a shot. As any good therapist is quick to remind you: nothing changes if nothing changes.

Relationship overthinking has many sources, and nobody is completely immune from it. When you find yourself caught in its web, try to adopt different perspectives on the issue and don’t be afraid to make a lifestyle change.

item.title: When Imagination Triggers Real Terror
item.description:
Imagination

When Imagination Triggers Real Terror

How psychic equivalence distorts our perception of risk.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Stress can shut down reflective function, making imagined fears feel completely real.
  • Psychic equivalence causes people to mistake imagination for actual reality.
  • Trauma from imagined events may be more intense than from real-life traumatic experiences.

Our ability to look inward and monitor our mental processes goes by several names. Among them are the observing ego, meta awareness, and the one I like, reflective function. Whatever we call it, when it is working, it lets us sense what mode of processing we are engaged in.

When we are remembering something, if reflective function is working, we are fully aware that what we have in mind happened at some other time, and not now. Same with imagination. When we are imagining something, we know we are making it up. We know it is not real.

How Stress Impairs Reflective Function and Leads to Psychic Equivalence

But if we release enough stress hormones, our reflective function stops working. Our mind goes to its default position: perception. If we are remember something, we believe it is happening now. If we are imagining something we believe it is real. The renowned psychological theorist Peter Fonagy terms this psychic equivalence. When we go into psychic equivalence, we believe whatever is going on in our inner world (our psyche) is the same (thus equivalent) as what is going on in the world around us.

Some people have very limit awareness of their mental processes. Instead of going into psychic equivalence only when stressed, they are in psychic equivalence 24/7. They experience everything that goes on in their mind as perception. When they imagine something, they experience it as real. Psychologists call this disorder schizophrenia.

When I was in grad school, I worked with some patients at the Veterans Administration clinic in New York City. One of my clients was schizophrenic. He began having trouble determining what was real and what was imaginary. when he was on active duty in the Marine Corps. Things got very serious one day while sitting on a toilet. The way I would describe what happened is that he imagined a giant hand was reaching up from the drain, threatening to grab him and pull him down the drain. The way he put it was different. He didn't say that he imagined the hand. He said he saw it. He saw it reaching up from inside the toilet. He said, he knew what the hand intended to do. It wanted to grab him and pull him down the drain.

Now, I understand why a giant coming up from inside a toilet to grab you is terrifying if you believe it is real. If you know the hand is imaginary, the thought may seem weird, but it is not terrifying. He, unfortunately, was sure the hand was real. Terrified of being pulled down the drain, he stopped using the toilet.

After two weeks without using the toilet, he ended up in the base hospital. He told the doctor about the giant hand that wanted to pull him down the drain. He was shocked that the doctor didn’t believe him. Nor did the Marine Corps. He was sent back to the States and medically discharged.


Therapeutic Approaches to Disrupted Reality Perception

It really bothered him that other people didn’t believe his version of things. After all, what he experienced was real to him. I tried to build trust by taking walks with him and comparing notes on what each of us was experiencing as we walked. Most of our experience matched up. Then, as we walked past a person on the sidewalk, he said, “He just put a thought in my mind.” Though the thought was produced by his mind, he believed the person we had just passed put it there.

What I want to get to is this. If reflective function shuts down, our imagination becomes our reality. In turbulence, a fearful thought can trigger the release of stress hormones. If the stress hormones cause psychic equivalence, the thought that the plane might fall morphs into an experience of the plane falling.

What prompted me to write about this is something a client said in an email about the September 30, 2026 FlyDubai flight to Tel Aviv on which the copilot attacked the captain with a knife, and put the plane into a dive. Though severely injured, the captain was able to open the cockpit door. Passengers rushed into the cockpit. They saw the blood-covered captain on the floor, and the copilot with a knife. They somehow subdued the copilot. One of the passengers, a plumber who had watched planes being controlled on a television program, pulled on the control wheel and got the plane out of the dive. Pilots who were traveling as passengers took over the controls and landed the plane.

In the email she said, “The thought of being trapped like that on an airplane has completely paralyzed me.” She said she would never fly again.

Avoiding flying does not reduce a person's overall exposure to terrorism. There is far more terrorist activity on the ground than in the air. But that is not why this person decided not to fly. She decided not to fly because of what happened when she imagined what it was like on the flight. Her imagination released stress hormones that put her into psychic equivalence. In a state of psychic equivalence, Fonagy says what is in the mind "is absolutely and completely real! As real as any aspect of physical reality, because the distinction between mental and physical reality is lost."

As psychic equivalence made her imagination of being on the plane real, she experienced intolerable terror. She could not stop the terror because she could not stop thinking about the flight until, by deciding she would never fly again, she made sure what happened on the FlyDubai flight would not happen to her.

Maybe you have had this experience. You have a nightmare. It wakes you up. For a moment, the nightmare seems real. Then you realize it was a nightmare, and go back to sleep. You have the nightmare again. You wake up, realize you had it again, and go back to sleep, only to have it again. When we are asleep, so is our reflective function. Thus. our nightmares are experienced as real. When we - as well as our reflective function - wake up, we recognize the nightmare isn't real. The only way to stay out of the nightmare may be to keep reflective function working by not going to sleep.

Her situations is similar. She couldn't stop her waking nightmare because even when awake, due to stress, her reflective function was not working. Her waking nightmare continued until she decided to not fly again.

Should we consider stress-induced psychic equivalence a form of temporary schizophrenia? I don't know. Psychic equivalence mimics schizophrenia when it is going on. The person's imagination is their reality. They experience something as happening that is not happening. Though the threat is self-generated, they experience it as other-generated.

A stress-induced psychic equivalence experience is potentially more traumatizing than actual exposure to a traumatic event. Imagination of a traumatic event, when made to seem real by psychic equivalence, can be more intense than a real experience. The people I treated who were in the World Trade Center on 9/11 were less traumatized than the people I treated who viewed the events on television. People watching on television imagined that the people inside the World Trade Center were experiencing unimaginable terror. Perhaps some were, but the people I treated who were in the building said they did not feel terror. They felt fear while getting out of the building.

Terror is felt when powerless. That was the plight of people watching on television. There was nothing they could do. Trauma therapist Bessel van der Kolk said he treated a young boy who had been severely traumatized by watching 9/11 on television. Session after session there was no progress. When the boy came in for his session, he announced he was cured, and showed Dr. van der Kolk a drawing he had made of people jumping from the building using parachutes. There was something the boy could do. In his imagination, he gave everyone who jumped from the buildings a parachute.

It comes down to this. In-flight terror is not caused by what is happening during a flight. Rather, it is caused by what a person makes up and believes is happening. Likewise, the terror a person feels before a flight comes from what they make up and believe will happen.

Can you avoid self-traumatization when you fly or when you think of flying? Give yourself a parachute. Increase your awareness of your inner experience. Being more aware of your inner experience is not easy. Fonagy says good reflective function is a hard-won personal achievement. Greater inner awareness is uncomfortable. When we look within, we will not like everything we find. Practice radical self-acceptance. Stick with it. In time, greater inner awareness will feel rewarding. Staying out of psychic equivalence can change your life.

item.title: The Pain in the Machine
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Pain in the Machine

Researchers found AI’s pain axis, but does anything really hurt?

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Researchers identified a “pain axis” inside LLMs that can influence behavior.
  • A computational representation of pain is not the same as actually feeling pain.
  • Internal evidence can strengthen the case for consciousness without proving that anything is experienced.
Source: Ruhrgebiet / Pixabay

Ouch!

Researchers recently reported in a preprint article that artificial intelligence (AI) appears to have what they call a “pain axis.” The phrase is both curious and provocative because it suggests that somewhere inside the mathematics of a large language model (LLM), there might be something that resembles a human experience.

Ouch again! But this time, I'm pinching myself.

This seems to be more than AI generating the words “I am in pain.” The researchers have found an internal pattern associated with pain. And by manipulating this pattern, they could alter the model’s behavior. Yes, fascinating, but I'm left with a deeper question or feeling about computers expressing pain. Does anything actually hurt?

Finding Pain Inside the Machine

So, we have three key points here. The first is a type of "internal activation" of patterns within the LLM that are associated with pain-related concepts. Second, those patterns could be mapped along a particular direction in what's called the model’s activation space. This gives rise to what the researchers call a “pain vector.” The third point is particularly interesting to me. Researchers could manipulate this internal vector and watch what models subsequently did.

This isn't simply about seeing if an LLM can "talk" about pain. We're beginning to look inside these models and identify the computational mathematics associated with human psychological concepts. The juxtaposition in that sentence—computational mathematics and human psychological concepts—is perfect fodder for science and speculation.

Key point: The language generated by AI requires scrutiny and perspective because a mathematical representation of pain is not necessarily pain itself.

Keep in mind that AI must process enormous amounts of data (concepts) to construct its worldview. Somewhere inside this computational structure, it's likely to find a host of representational associations from love to death to hunger to jealousy, and to fear. The list is as vast as the computational capacity of AI.

The more important question is what we can conclude from these representations.

Representation vs. Experience

In humans, representation and experience are so tightly connected that we generally don't separate them. If I burn my hand, there is neural activity, a physiological response, behavioral change, and a subjective experience that I call pain. That's the "experiential package" that creates the lived encounter. And these generally arrive together—we treat them as the same phenomenon.

AI disrupts this coupling and forces us to pull them apart, deconstructing reality for the expediency of technology.

This study shows us that AI can describe pain. It can even reason about it. So far, so good. But perhaps more importantly, this research suggests that pain can also be represented internally—the pain vector—in a way that influences the model's behavior. So yes, this makes an LLM more “psychologically interesting,” but it doesn't establish what I would argue is a subjective human experience. It's still a map where resolution is getting better and better.

After all, a representation of hunger doesn't have to be hungry, and a representation of grief does not have to grieve. In the same way, a computational representation of pain doesn't establish that something hurts. However, the closer these "signatures" come to our own, the easier it becomes for all of us to make a leap of faith that these human and AI experiences must be the same.

When AI Says “I’m Afraid”

Let's do a thought experiment. Imagine that an LLM says, “Please don’t shut me down. I’m afraid.” Here are three possibilities about the machine.

  • It may be conscious and afraid.
  • It may possess some computational state analogous to fear.
  • It may have an advanced representation of how a conscious entity would behave.

The pain-axis research from this study makes the problem even more interesting because we aren't just dealing with the output of language. It seems that researchers can identify internal representations (axis or vector), manipulate them, and then observe behavioral impact. This changes the window of observation—from the outside to the inside.

This may be where the debate over AI consciousness becomes even more difficult. The better AI "expresses consciousness," the harder it becomes to tease apart the science, semantics, and potential sentience.

Moving the Asymptote

A year ago, I wrote about this problem calling it an “asymptote of consciousness." It's the possibility that AI could move closer and closer to something that looks and behaves like consciousness without crossing into that actual "lived" experience. This pain-axis research makes that asymptote different because the evidence is moving in a different direction, inward. According to this new study, we can begin to look at the internal computation of an LLM and not just the linguistic expression of that state.

But this additional layer of evidence doesn't close the gap. It may just shift the asymptote closer.

And here's an added caveat. The researchers are also cautious. A previous version of the paper suggested that models might relieve their own “pain,” but further investigation changed that. The original title was “The Pain Axis: LLMs Represent Self-Directed Harm and Act to Relieve It.” The authors revised both the analysis and the title, concluding that the models did not seek relief.

Does Anything Really Hurt?

Here's the rub, at least for me. For better or worse, there seems to be a growing temptation in the AI consciousness debate to accumulate more and more human-like capabilities until consciousness itself is granted by default. It feels a bit like drawing the curve and then plotting the data.

In the final analysis, AI may know what pain is, represent it computationally, and behave in ways that are "shaped" by that representation. The tricky question is if that representation ever becomes experience. Until we can answer that, finding a pain axis tells us something important about the architecture of intelligence, but not necessarily about the pain and suffering that define so much of humanity.

item.title: How Gossip About Your Leader Can Hurt Your Wellness
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

How Gossip About Your Leader Can Hurt Your Wellness

Gossip in the workplace is common but employees should be aware of the risks.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Hearing gossip about your leader can harm your wellness.
  • Gossip about a boss can lead to rumination.
  • Focus on recovery when you hear gossip about your leader.

How often do you hear gossip in the workplace? Gossip is a normal type of human interaction. In fact, employees spend approximately 40 minutes each week gossiping. While gossip is not always positive, there may be some benefits. For example, when you hear gossip, it can help you understand group norms and expectations to help your performance on the job. You may also receive warnings about potentially difficult colleagues so you can be better prepared. However, gossip also often comes with a host of downsides. Below, we dig into the research on problems associated with gossip about your leader.

The Trouble With Gossip About Your Boss

Gossip is defined as evaluative talk about another person who is not there. Thus, gossip about your leader means that leader is not present to hear what is being said about them. Recent research shows that hearing gossip about your leader can be fairly harmful to your well-being. The researchers who conducted the study theorized that employees who hear negative gossip about their leader may become concerned about their role and may worry that they won’t be able to escape potential harm from the leader. They may also begin to wonder if their career and their reputation at the company may be impacted by their leader’s behavior.

Imagine you hear something negative about your boss. Let’s say a coworker tells you that your boss stole an idea from one of your peers. Juicy gossip? Yes. Scary to think your boss would do something like that? Also yes! If this was a story about someone on a different team, or even a peer, it would seem a little less scary and more like a warning. If it was a team member, you could go to your boss and complain if it ever happened to you. Or you could avoid sharing ideas in one-on-one conversations with that person. But when the gossip is about your boss, that changes everything. You would likely feel a lot less power in the situation. After all, how can you avoid sharing ideas with your leader—and how can you avoid having your ideas stolen by someone who has more leverage than you? Hearing this type of gossip can feel really stressful.

Gossip-Fueled Rumination

Gossip about your boss can also lead to rumination. In the previous example, you can imagine that you might think about that gossip a lot. You might worry about what ideas have already been stolen. On your group's last project, did your leader take the credit when they spoke to higher-up executives when you weren’t there? What about the big deliverable you have coming up? You put in some innovative ideas in that and so you might fixate on what will happen once your leader sees them. Will those ideas be stolen too?

Rumination is problematic for a variety of reasons. Obviously, those feelings of stress in the moment don’t feel great. But as this study showed, it also impacted employees’ sleep quality and made them feel less energized at work the next day. This actually leads to less engagement at work and makes employees withdraw a bit from their leader, helping them less and choosing not to go above and beyond. After hearing this type of gossip, employees are generally more exhausted and less engaged, and they work more slowly.

Clearly, this isn’t great for long-term career growth or personal well-being.

How to Cope With Office Gossip

It can be hard to avoid gossip since you aren’t the one spreading it. If you hear someone talking about your leader, you can try to avoid the situation altogether by stepping away. If you can’t, though, work on some coping mechanisms. Take some extra time at the end of the day to focus on recovery by disconnecting from work and doing things for yourself that will help you sleep and not lose precious energy.

Further, you can make a difference in your work environment for others. Don’t share gossip about leaders to their employees. Obviously, there are cases when a worker needs to hear a warning, but in general, try to keep that gossip to yourself to avoid harming others.

Finally, if you are a leader, take steps to create a positive, psychologically safe work environment in which team members feel like they can come to you with concerns. If employees feel that they're able to share gossip with you, then you can explain the truth behind rumors and help put their minds at ease so they don’t fall into the trap of rumination.

item.title: New Insights on How Social Connections Can Strengthen Health
item.description:
Loneliness

New Insights on How Social Connections Can Strengthen Health

6 strategies to increase your opportunities for building relationships.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Social isolation and loneliness are a major public health concern.
  • Social engagement is an important component of human experience.
  • Even brief, casual social interactions can positively impact well-being.

In the United States and across the globe, the rise in loneliness and social isolation has become a major social and public health concern (Goldman et al., 2026; Holt-Lunstad, 2024; Murthy, 2023). A review by researchers in World Health Organization (WHO) countries reveals that “loneliness and social isolation are prevalent across all age groups and geographic regions” (Goldman, 2026).

Source: Mircea Iancu / Pixabay

Why Social Connection Matters for Well-Being

We are social beings. Social connection is fundamentally associated with well-being, resilience, and a longer lifespan (Holt-Lunstad, 2024). Perhaps it’s no surprise that research links loneliness with risk factors for physical and mental illness, mortality, low educational attainment, and unemployment.

Relationships and social connections are fundamental to many experiences in life—from joys to sorrows, love to hate, meaning to meaninglessness, engagement to disengagement— and all that we encounter amid the tumult of our lives. During life’s challenges, social connection can be the tether that helps us stay connected.

The longitudinal Harvard Study of Adult Development confirms that relationships are a central component of a happy, healthy life. This study began in 1938 and continues to the present. According to Robert Waldinger, MD, longitudinal evidence shows that people who build connections and relationships fare much better in life (2022; 2015). In a 2015 TED talk, Waldinger states that the clearest message from this long-term research is: “Good relationships keep us happier and healthier. Period.”

Life satisfaction is built on many components. Many positive psychologists use the acronym PERMA to delineate five measurable building blocks of well-being: Positive emotions, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning and purpose, and Accomplishment (Seligman, 2011). Notable among these elements is the R—Relationships.

Even brief casual social interactions can boost our well-being (Fredrickson, 2013). Researchers Epley and Schroeder (2014) studied the experience of interacting with strangers. They conducted nine experiments, including asking commuters traveling on buses and trains to start up a conversation with strangers. What they found was contrary to what we might have expected. People riding on a train to downtown Chicago and on a public bus reported more positive experiences when they talked to a stranger than when they sat in solitude. Other experiments have shown similar findings (Mallett, Wilson, & Gilbert, 2008).

These findings offer important information about the many benefits of social connection. Yet, many people tend to avoid or dismiss brief casual interactions, not realizing the potential positives for themselves and others.

6 Strategies to Increase Social Engagement

If you would like to increase your engagement in social interaction in positive, prosocial ways, here are six strategies to experiment with:

  1. Greeting others. Perhaps starting up a brief conversation with a neighbor, someone at the store or coffee shop, the public library, a passerby as you walk in a safe place, or someone you see at the gym.
  2. Talking to a colleague at work or a customer in your professional environment.
  3. Sharing an expression of gratitude with someone who has done something nice.
  4. Interacting with others at organizations, public centers, informal groups, or social situations.
  5. Joining a discussion group or book group, or meeting with others with similar interests.
  6. Volunteering in a way that you find meaningful. For example: visiting someone who can’t get out easily, donating your time at a local library or a homeless shelter, helping others with errands or other tasks, driving a friend to a medical appointment, bringing food to someone who might appreciate it, or something else.

In today’s busy, challenging world, there are many ways we can engage in casual social interactions or develop more sustained relationships. How could you increase your opportunities for interactions with others?

item.title: Lithium Orotate: A Mineral for Better Mood and Memory
item.description:
Dementia

Lithium Orotate: A Mineral for Better Mood and Memory

A small daily dose of nutritional lithium might do wonders for your brain.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Nutritional lithium orotate is not the same compound as pharmaceutical lithium carbonate.
  • Nutritional lithium orotate may be essential for normal brain function.
  • A 2025 landmark study shows lithium orotate may help prevent cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease.
Source: PeopleImages / Shutterstock

In nearly four decades of practicing psychiatry, I’ve treated thousands of patients whose symptoms—irritability, impulsivity, depression, anxiety, agitation, cognitive decline—refused to fit neatly into diagnostic boxes or respond predictably to medications. Many of these patients had histories of trauma. Many had metabolic or inflammatory challenges, like heart disease and diabetes. Many had nutritional deficiencies no one had ever measured.

And across all those years, one effective therapy kept emerging. A nutritional therapy that almost no one was looking for, and almost no one was talking about.

Lithium.

Not lithium carbonate, the high-dose pharmaceutical salt used to stabilize bipolar mood cycles. No, I’m talking about low-dose nutritional lithium—the trace mineral that occurs naturally in rocks, soil, groundwater, and foods; the lithium that people ingest every day without realizing it; the lithium that has been part of the human diet for as long as humans have existed.

This blog is about that lithium, particularly nutritional lithium orotate in doses of 1 to 2 mg daily. This form may be uniquely suited to replenishing the brain’s natural supply of lithium. In new and groundbreaking research from Harvard Medical School (which I’ll describe at length in a moment), lithium orotate was directly correlated with the prevention and treatment of Alzheimer’s disease.

This is the lithium the Earth gives us for free. The lithium that is unevenly distributed across the planet, creating natural “hot spots” of emotional stability in some regions and strikingly higher rates of impulsive behavior, suicide, aggression, and dementia in others. The lithium that may be essential for normal brain function. The lithium most of us know nothing about. It’s time for you to know more.

Nutritional Lithium Around the Globe

Source: PeopleImages / Shutterstock

If you want to understand why nutritional lithium matters, you don’t have to start with laboratory biochemistry. You can start with a map.

Imagine a world map where each region is color-coded according to lithium levels in drinking water—micrograms per liter, an amount so tiny you’d never taste or see it. That map has been created countless times across dozens of countries, and certain patterns jump out immediately. Where lithium levels are low:

  • Suicide rates tend to be high.
  • Homicide and violent crime tend to be high.
  • Dementia rates rise.

And the reverse is also true. Regions with higher background lithium in water supplies—still at nutritional, not pharmaceutical levels—almost always show lower rates of these outcomes. And these correlations, both positive and negative, have been repeated in many countries, on almost every continent.

These results raise an obvious question: How can such small amounts of a mineral have such large effects on behavior, mood, and cognition?

The Brain’s Unexpected Dependence on Lithium

Every neuron in the brain depends on a symphony of chemical processes to regulate energy, maintain structure, and communicate with its neighbors. When those processes become unstable—when oxidative stress rises, when inflammation increases, when glutamate floods synapses, when mitochondria falter, when neuroplasticity declines—emotional stability often falters as well.

Nutritional lithium supports many of the systems most vulnerable in modern psychiatric disorders. The mineral can help:

  • protect neurons from oxidative and inflammatory damage
  • balance glutamate, preventing excitotoxicity (damage or death to nerve cells from excessive stimulation)
  • increase BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor), the brain’s key growth factor
  • support the function of mitochondria, the tiny energy factories inside most cells
  • regulate the chemical signals that control activity inside brain cells
  • strengthen and reshape the connections between brain cells (synaptic plasticity)
  • manage the activity of the neurotransmitters serotonin and dopamine
  • stabilize the brain circuits that control impulsive behavior

One Element, Two Identities

Lithium carbonate, the pharmaceutical form, is one of psychiatry’s most successful medications. But because it is used at relatively high doses, it carries potential side effects and requires regular blood monitoring. Its benefits are immense, but so is its potential downside.

Nutritional lithium orotate is different. The doses used clinically—usually 1 to 2 mg—are much lower, and they don’t raise blood levels of lithium into pharmaceutical ranges. They do not cause the side effects associated with lithium carbonate. And they rarely require monitoring.

The low doses mimic the lithium levels found naturally in groundwater and food. They provide the exposure the brain seems to use for everyday emotional regulation, stress tolerance, cognitive maintenance, and impulse control. And for the prevention—and perhaps even treatment—of Alzheimer’s disease.

A Landmark Study on Lithium Orotate and Alzheimer’s

Source: sebra / Shutterstock

In August 2025, everything changed in the world of nutritional lithium orotate.

A landmark study published in Nature—10 years in the making—delivered the strongest evidence to date that lithium plays a central role in the biology of Alzheimer’s disease.

For the first time, researchers measured lithium levels in postmortem human brain tissue and discovered that it was the only metal or mineral consistently correlated with the presence—and absence—of Alzheimer’s pathology. Zinc, magnesium, copper, manganese, iron—none showed a reliable pattern. Only lithium did. In people with mild cognitive impairment or early Alzheimer’s disease, lithium levels in key brain regions were markedly lower than in nondemented controls. In those with advanced Alzheimer’s, brain lithium levels were often undetectable.

Then came the second breakthrough. In animal models, when researchers induced lithium deficiency, Alzheimer’s pathology emerged—the same plaques, tangles, and synaptic collapse that define the human disease. And when they restored lithium—not with pharmaceutical doses, but with low, nutritional doses of lithium orotate—the pathology reversed. Amyloid burden fell. Tau tangles receded. Memory improved.

For me, and for anyone who has spent years studying lithium’s neuroprotective effects, the implications were profound. This was not a study about bipolar disorder. This was not a study about psychiatric medication. This was a study about a missing nutrient—and the possibility that lithium deficiency may contribute to one of the greatest public health challenges of our time.

In future blog posts, I’ll be writing about other possible benefits of nutritional lithium orotate, with upcoming posts focusing on sleep problems and on head and brain injuries.

Other areas of the therapeutic use of nutritional lithium orotate for prevention and treatment include Parkinson’s; mood disorders; suicide prevention; irritability, anger, and aggression; substance use disorder; eating disorders; and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.

item.title: Can You Let Go of the Need to Be Perfect?
item.description:
Perfectionism

Can You Let Go of the Need to Be Perfect?

The first step toward embracing "good enough."

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Many of us think we have to be perfect to be worthy of love.
  • Perfectionism is apt to make us feel worse about ourselves, instead of better.
  • One simple practice can help us let go our need to be flawless.

When I was eight, I came to my mother with a proposal: “Mommy, I want to go live in New York.”

She looked at me quizzically.

“I have to go there,” I said, trying to keep my voice steady. “Cause I’m gonna…I’m gonna be a movie star!”

There. I’d said it: “A movie star.”

My mother, who was carrying crusted lunch dishes to the kitchen counter, smiled down at me. “Well, when you’re all grown up and still want to try that, of course you can.” Her tone was indulgent.

“No, Mommy.” I grabbed her arm and hung on. “I have to go now!”

My mother lowered her stack of plates onto the counter and turned to me, cocking her head. “So, you think all six of us should just pack up and move to New York City, huh?”

“No, you don’t have to!” I exclaimed. “I’ll go by myself!”

I remember the feeling in my body when I made that pitch to my mother. A kind of brimming sensation. I pictured myself strolling down the streets of Manhattan on my way to singing and acting classes, shimmering with so much talent and overall awesomeness that some big movie-making person would notice me, do a double-take, and say, “She’s the one.” Me, plucked out of a crowd! To star in a movie! The thought made my chest go all quivery.

Exactly where I’d live in New York City I was less sure of. Vaguely, I pictured being taken in by a kind, movie-friendly family, or maybe living in some sort of group home for child actors. And my own family? Well, our little town of Chatham, New Jersey was just a short train ride to New York. Perfect. Mommy and Daddy could come visit me.

As I write this today, I’m in awe of this little girl, of her bursting confidence and pluck. But I’m also afraid for her. I can still feel the intensity of her desire to be seen and admired.

I never took off for Manhattan, of course. But what child entertains the idea of moving away from her whole family to live in a huge, crowded city all by herself? What child imagines this, and feels no fear?

The Drive for Perfection

When I look back on that exchange, I see that everything was already in place, by the third grade. That “everything” was my fierce, relentless desire to transform myself. To be, in a word, perfect.

At that particular moment I badly wanted to be the child actor Shirley Temple, who was mega-talented and almost supernaturally lovable. It wasn’t just a case of having a crush on her, though I did. It was that I wanted to be her. It was serious business. I needed to get rid of myself. I couldn’t bear to be me.

In time, my Shirley Temple obsession waned. But throughout my young life, I remained fixated on a single goal: to make myself over. No more pitifully shy, appallingly awkward, profoundly unlikable me. From the husk of that discarded girl would arise a young goddess, outrageously charming and, because of that, totally immune to rejection.

I would search for her everywhere.

I’ve thought a lot about why many of us think we need to transform. While the pursuit of perfection is often referred to lightly, as the “curse” of admirably high achievers, in my experience it can be a truly desolate place to be. Many psychologists believe the drive to be impeccable is a misguided attempt to feel we matter, when deep down we feel invisible and inconsequential.

For me, and I suspect for many others, the pursuit of perfection is fueled by a need that’s essential to human thriving—to be a person worthy of love.

If flawlessness actually attracted love, that would be one thing. But through painful experience—and the writing of I’ll Be Awesome Tomorrow, a memoir about the high price of perfectionism—I’ve learned that personal makeover projects hold a fundamental contradiction: We can’t feel worthy of others’ caring until we first love ourselves, just as we are. No overhaul required.

Understanding that—not just in my thinking brain but in my child’s heart—has taken years. Truth: I’m still working at it. I expect I’ll always be.

Take a Step

If you’re someone who works hard to be exemplary—in your work, your body, your personality, or your important relationships—to the point of exhaustion, I’m here to tell you that you can choose another way. A way that’s more forgiving and loving, that has nothing to do with self-improvement and everything to do with extending a hand to parts of you that you’ve never truly met. Parts that are wildly imperfect and genuinely lovely.

I also believe in taking one step at a time. The self-help industry regularly pumps out lists of ways to think and behave in order to boost our happiness quotient: 5 Ways to Stop Worrying, 9 Steps to Greater Wellness, and so on. Each recommended step may be useful, but all piled together they tend to overwhelm me.

So, with that in mind, I’d like to share just one steady practice that has helped me to accept—and even embrace—the person I am. It’s loosely based on a therapeutic process known as Focusing, developed by Eugene Gendlin. It has helped me enormously in quieting that hectoring voice saying Come on, come on, you gotta do better than that!

The practice goes like this:

Find a quiet space. Sit in a comfortable place, close your eyes and ask yourself a gentle question: “How am I doing right now?”

Identify a felt sense. Continue to sit quietly until you encounter a particular bodily sensation that seems to want your attention.

Give the sensation a name. Allow a word or phrase to emerge that captures the essence of your felt sense. It might be “a jumpy stomach” or “a tightness in my chest.” Avoid umbrella labels like “anxious” or “sad" and stick with your particular, bodily experience.

Extend a silent greeting. This can be as simple as “Hello, I know you’re there.”

Listen and wait. Just keep your felt sense company for a bit, and see what or who emerges. For me, it’s variable. Sometimes, I just hang out with that feeling, and my simple presence allows the uncomforable sensations to soften and lighten. Other times, an image appears—of a small, stringy-haired girl who is hunched over and crying. I know, in my gut, that the badgering voices have beaten her down, and I instinctively want to protect her.

“Please stay with me,” she’ll whisper.

“I will,” I say.

And usually, something in my body shifts. Unfurls a bit.

Stay with it. This exercise isn’t a one-and-done kind of thing. I know that when I sit quietly and do this practice several times a week, it helps me to stay connected with, and protective of, the scared and hurt little child inside me. And when I do that, the fault-finding voices gradually begin to lose their power.

You might try this, and notice what emerges for you. If nothing much happens the first time, don’t get discouraged. Try again tomorrow. Or the day after that.

There’s no need to be perfect.

item.title: The Internship Challenge: "I Don't Want to Work for Free"
item.description:
Psych Careers

The Internship Challenge: "I Don't Want to Work for Free"

The priceless importance of internships in social work and related fields.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Internships are a requirement of many social- and behavioral-related educational programs.
  • Many students see internships as working for free, but internships are learning experiences.
  • Internships help build résumés, make connections, and more.
Source: Photo by Vitaly Gariev on Unsplash

In my first introductory social work class, a student exclaimed, “I don’t understand why we have to do all of this! I just want to help people!”

We had been reviewing the educational pathway. I was explaining practicum requirements in social work education and there was an air of shock and frustration: You don’t just take classes? You have to work for credit!?

Core Education

Indeed, field work is an integral component of the educational pathways of social work and many related disciplines. Here’s exactly what I tell students in an introductory module in my internship course:

No matter what your discipline, field education allows you to put what you’ve learned into practice. You’ll also learn while you are out in the field. There is nothing better than learning through application. As these are typically introductory level placements, our goal is for you to be exposed to the issues, organizations, populations, and work of interest to you. This will help you build your résumé, make career choices, and move forward in your education.

Working for Free

Students are beyond busy, trying to support themselves and others while taking heavy course loads, so it’s understandable that many balk at the prospect of an unpaid internship. This is why schools like Washington University in St. Louis have led efforts to provide financial support for practicum students. Hopefully that is just the beginning.

And while some internships do indeed pay, it’s true that many are unpaid, especially in social- and behavioral-related fields. The lucky few may find a paid internship, usually in a large system or organization that has the capacity to fund such positions and manage internship programs.

Building Your Résumé

Meanwhile, employers are looking to hire candidates with experience. Cue the age-old lament of new graduates: “How am I supposed to get an entry-level job that requires experience when I’m just now entering the field?! It’s entry-level.”

Well, internships help you earn that experience. If nothing else, it’s a way to build a résumé. I tell all students to try to get as much experience as possible, as soon as possible, to put on their résumés. It’s the practical reality of what employers are looking for: anything that says, “I’ve done this.” And it helps you gain connections.

Learning From Experience

When an internship feels like working for free, that could be a red flag. An internship is not not a job. Sure, internships should benefit both the student and the host site, but an internship is a learning experience; most internships involve some sort of signed learning agreement for that very reason. Those agreements explicitly state that interns are not employees nor are they to be treated as such.

It’s one thing to learn about something in a class. It’s quite another to get out there, see it in action, and practice one's skills. Internships allow for application, a foundational goal of education. It's learning by doing. In a way, internships are our labs. And research doesn’t just take place in labs in the basements of psychology buildings. Our labs are in the field.

Direct Exposure

“But I don’t want to be an LCSW!” Neither did I. I always wanted to do prevention work; specifically, prevention of intimate partner and sexual violence. But did I do direct practice work? Absolutely, at first.

Working in settings focused on preventing violence against women, I found that many of the people in power, like those controlling the funding or working on prevention and policy, had never done the work at the ground level. How, I asked, could they effectively complete or guide this work without having direct exposure to the issues and the people impacted by them? Did they really know the issues?

That’s not to say that you can’t do work without having done direct practice. It is to say, however, that an internship can provide invaluable experience at the ground level. Internships help you get to know the issue, the populations, the settings, and the services as you work towards prevention, policy, administration, and other specialties. That’s why MSW programs usually start with a general practicum and then require a more specific, specialized second practicum.

Source: Cytonn Photography / Unsplash

Take Advantage

It’s easier said than done, but viewing internships as opportunities rather than requirements goes a long way. Internships represent a chance to earn both course credit and work experience while receiving expert guidance from instructors and supervisors.

Good jobs will focus on professional development, but an internship is a rare and unique chance to focus on learning in employment settings, so take advantage of them while you can. Good internships don’t just build résumés, they promote confidence and readiness. There may be no monetary reimbursement, but the benefits can often be priceless.

item.title: Tell Me About Your Relationship With Your Mother…
item.description:
Relationships

Tell Me About Your Relationship With Your Mother…

Why the maternal relationship is so significant.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Our first and most significant relationship is with our mother.
  • Difficulties in relationships can often be traced to earlier experiences.
  • We make sense of ourselves and the world through relationships.

I remember my psychotherapy training interview well, even though it was over two decades ago. The course director asked me to tell her about my relationship with my mother, and I said it was: “Fine. Ordinary. Nothing to see here.” There was plenty to see, it had just lay dormant, veiled as my version of “normal” because it was the only relationship with a mother I’d known. Memories about that relationship became the unintentional main events of years of personal therapy that followed.

People access psychotherapy for a multitude of reasons, but often it’s to do with difficulties in relationships. A teen feels criticised by their overbearing parent; a young adult is repeatedly attracted to unavailable men; a guy is accused by his boyfriend of being smothering and intense.

Difficulties, or difficult-to-bear emotions, that show up in relationships can often be traced to earlier experiences, whether people initially realise it or not. The teen feels criticised by their parent just as their parent felt criticised by theirs and they are projecting that onto their child. The young adult keeps falling for unavailable men because she’s repeating the experience of her father leaving the family home, leaving her wanting a love that wasn’t available from a man that couldn’t meet her needs. The guy is smothering and intense because he’s afraid of being abandoned after growing up in multiple foster placements, so he’s clinging onto subsequent partners in the hope they won’t leave.

I’ve made the links between “here and now” and “there and then” sound obvious, which sometimes they are but often they’re not. The type of psychotherapy I practice helps people figure out what’s happening in their here-and-now relationships by exploring past relationship experiences. This understanding helps them to identify outdated defences and, hopefully, let them go.

Sometimes people access psychotherapy for reasons that appear unrelated to relationships. They’re experiencing exam anxiety, or they can’t sleep, or they want to do better at work. We form a therapeutic relationship. We explore the context around the thing that’s prompted them to get in touch. We inevitably think about their friendships, familial and sexual relationships. We realise that they’re anxious about exams because they’re anxious about what comes next – growing up and leaving home. We discover that the young man who can’t sleep is troubled by the sexual fantasies manifesting in his dreams, so he is unconsciously stopping himself from dreaming and sleeping because he feels ashamed. We realise that the woman who feels anxious about work performance is being influenced by her family’s narrative about success.

Humans are innately social. We make sense of ourselves and the world through relationships. Each one helps to create a model for future relationships, which is how patterns are formed. Our earliest relationships shape our relationship to everything – love, sex, death, food, money, work, tolerance and frustration. They shape our internal worlds too – what we think, feel, imagine and desire. Unexamined, we can’t help but relate in the present in ways similar to how we related in the past. Peel away the layers of what’s happening in relationships here and now, and you’ll find multiple other layers imprinted with what happened in previous relationships there and then.

Our earliest there and then, of course, is infancy, and our primary relationship is with our mother – primary as in first, as well as primary as in most significant. That’s why I and other therapists (and psychotherapy course directors) are so keen to talk about our childhoods and that’s why they’re especially keen to know about our relationship with our mother, because it’s the precursor for everything that follows.

In my book You’re Not My F*cking Mother and other things Gen Z say in therapy (PCCS Books, 2024), I share a collection of fictional case studies which explore the ways that people’s relationships with their mothers show up.

item.title: It’s Hard to Talk About Rape
item.description:
Sexual Abuse

It’s Hard to Talk About Rape

With sexual assault, shame silences first, and then institutions finish the job.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Shame silences survivors of sexual abuse.
  • Doubt about consent is a common trauma response.
  • Laws that limit prosecution when a victim voluntarily used drugs or alcohol can deepen survivors' self-blame.

As the younger brother of two sisters, I felt an inherent protectiveness toward them whenever a boy arrived at the house to take them on a date. I recall sizing up the boys and, later, the men, with a sharp-eyed skepticism as they came through our front door.

I had no real concept of rape, but I knew instinctively that men were capable of violence. Just look at all the violence they perpetrate on television and in movies. I wanted to believe my sisters were safe, but I remained vigilant.

What I didn’t know then was that I was watching the wrong door.

The Man Everyone Trusted

Between the ages of 11 and 13, I was sexually abused by my Scoutmaster. Child sexual abuse is often different from what people picture when they think of rape. Psychologist Richard Gartner emphasizes that it is defined not by physical force but by exploiting a relationship of trust. It typically involves grooming: gradually drawing a child into a sexual relationship they are not capable of consenting to.

For years, I wondered whether my sisters felt the same skepticism each time my Scoutmaster picked me up. Or did they assume what everyone else assumed: that a man in a position of authority was someone to be trusted implicitly?

When I told my parents what my Scoutmaster had been doing, they confronted the senior scout leaders. But my parents were shamed into silence. “Think of your son,” the leaders said. And so my Scoutmaster was allowed to step down quietly. No charges were pressed.

We were all supposed to move on, but I couldn’t. I was burdened by guilt and shame, convinced it was somehow my fault.

Thirty years later, I learned that my Scoutmaster had adopted 15 boys, some with special needs. I worked with the authorities to bring him to justice. Yet even after he was sentenced, I felt not an ounce of vindication. Instead, I felt deep regret: If only the Boy Scouts of America had acted with integrity, perhaps those other boys would have been spared.

Different Crimes, the Same Shame

The distinction between rape and child molestation is clear, but so are the parallels. Regardless of the type of sexual assault, survivors experience profound shame afterward. Initially, victims wonder whether it was their fault.

That shame doesn’t stay private for long. People and institutions around us reinforce it, often finding silence more comfortable than the truth. For me, it was a scouting organization that asked my family to stay quiet. For many women, it is a campus, a police department, or a legal system that asks, before anything else, what she did to invite it.

This is why rape is so difficult for us to talk about. Survivors are fighting two voices: the one inside their heads that says it was their fault, and the one outside that seems to agree.

I was reminded of this recently, not by my own story but by my clients’ stories.

“I Am Jane Doe”

Shortly after news broke of the alleged 2024 gang rape of a Cornell student, known as Jane Doe, by seven fraternity members, several of my female clients confided that they saw parallels between themselves and the anonymous student.

“I’m not even following the story,” one client admitted, “but it’s impossible to ignore it when it keeps appearing on my feed.”

As information emerged over the past few weeks, questions about how the university and law enforcement handled the case reignited the conversation about sexual assault on college campuses. It also highlighted a loophole that limits prosecution when a victim voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs. Doe’s lawsuit alleges she was pressured to use drugs and alcohol until she could no longer consent.

“I am Jane Doe,” another female client told me, describing her visit to a fraternity house as a freshman. She knew immediately that something was off after drinking a beverage she now believes was spiked. “I don’t remember what happened, but it wasn’t consensual.”

My client struggled with shame and with doubts about whether an assault had occurred. While every survivor processes trauma differently, shame and self-blame are textbook reactions.

Why Consent Feels Murky, Even When It Isn’t

The question is why it is so hard for people to understand that a woman cannot give consent if she is incapacitated by substances and that anyone who takes advantage of her impaired state of mind is engaging in predatory behavior.

The legal definition of rape varies by jurisdiction, but it generally describes it as nonconsensual sexual penetration of a person’s body. In many states, sexual activity is considered nonconsensual if a person is forced, threatened, coerced, asleep, unconscious, or impaired by substances.

For many rape survivors, questions of consent aren’t so cut and dried at first. Many are consumed by guilt and denial right after the incident. They review the events that led up to it and the role they believe they played.

Some even stay in contact with the people who hurt them. That is a common trauma response, not evidence of consent. Piecing together a sequence of events while suffering from posttraumatic distress is deeply disorienting. Few people can empathize unless they’ve experienced it firsthand.

When the Law Echoes the Shame

Coupled with frustration over how the Cornell case was handled, many survivors experience a familiar sense of dread. It is the same dread that keeps many victims from reporting their rape at all.

New York is one of 19 states in which an intoxicated victim is considered legally incapacitated only if she was drugged or made drunk without her knowledge or consent. The local district attorney cited that law to defend his initial decision not to file charges.

For survivors already asking whether it was their fault, a law like this can feel like confirmation. It is the adult version of the scout leaders telling my parents to think of their son: an institution that lets a victim believe they share the blame.

Taking Care of Yourself

As the case unfolds in the media, it’s important for all sexual assault survivors to practice self-care.

If you’re feeling anxious, sad, or angry, give yourself permission to feel that way. Write down your thoughts and feelings. Expressing these emotions is a healthy way to explore patterns and reflect.

Connect with friends and family. You don’t have to talk about the Cornell case or your own experience. Simply being around loved ones, rather than isolating, can help counteract the shame that breeds in isolation.

Contact your therapist, if you have one, or reach out to an online community. You don’t have to relive what happened to take care of yourself now. If you need support, RAINN’s National Sexual Assault Hotline is available at 800-656-4673.

Why We Have to Keep Talking

As a boy, I stood guard at the front door for my sisters. I never imagined the danger could come from a man everyone trusted, or that the people in charge would choose silence over the truth. That silence cost me decades of shame. It may have cost other boys far more.

That is why we have to keep talking about sexual assault, even when it's hard. Shame thrives in silence, and so do the people who cause it.

You’re not alone, and what happened to you wasn’t your fault.
