item.title: Your Brain on AI: Why We Must Choose What We Outsource
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Your Brain on AI: Why We Must Choose What We Outsource

Which tasks should you hand to AI, and which should you keep for yourself?

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Our brains are "cognitive misers." So GenAI makes it increasingly tempting to outsource our thinking.
  • The less we use our brains to think and make decisions, the less capable they become, even with deep expertise
  • Judgment and critical thinking, the skills we need to decide when to trust AI, are among the most at risk.
  • Before outsourcing, ask #1. If the skill matters? #2. If you could defend the output? #3. What you'd lose?

When did you last write an important email without asking AI to improve it, if not write the whole thing for you?

For many people, it's been a while. Drafting messages. Brainstorming ideas. Preparing presentations. Even helping make a tough decision. Tasks we once did without a second thought now start with a prompt. And there's a good reason why. We're all pressed for time, and GenAI is fast.

None of this would be a problem, except that somewhere between our first dabble with GenAI and today, the handy assist became a habit. And while we shape our habits, over time our habits shape us. Not always for the better.

Our brains are wired to take the easier option. AI has paved it.

Social psychologists Susan Fiske and Shelley Taylor coined the term "cognitive misers" to describe our natural tendency to conserve mental effort wherever we can. It's not laziness. It's an intelligent adaptation that has served us well for millennia. So when our smartest thinking produces a tool that can think for us, doing in seconds what might otherwise take hours, our brains don't just accept the offer. They leap at it.

You've likely heard the catchphrase "Neurons that fire together, wire together." The more our neurons do a task, the better they get at it. Yet the flip side is also true. Just as your muscles weaken when you stop going to the gym, your brain is no exception. Use it or lose it.

The Problem: If Our Brains Aren't Regularly Thinking, They're Shrinking

Consider London's taxi drivers. To earn their license, they spend years memorizing some 25,000 streets. Brain scans show the region tied to spatial memory is larger in their brains than in non-drivers'. Meanwhile, research from McGill University found that people who lean heavily on GPS have weaker spatial memory. Same brain, different habits, different results.

AI appears to work the same way. Researchers at MIT used EEG to monitor people writing essays with ChatGPT, a search engine, or no tools at all. Those writing unaided showed the strongest brain connectivity. ChatGPT users showed the weakest, and felt the least ownership of their work. The researchers called this "cognitive debt": convenience now, cost later. The study was small and not yet peer-reviewed, but a survey by Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon University points the same way: the more people trusted AI with a task, the less critically they thought about it.

Once an afternoon's work takes 30 seconds, going back to the old way feels like returning to washing dishes by hand after years with a dishwasher. Our brains may be misers, but they are also little Einsteins at rationalizing why the faster option is the smarter one.

The Most Important Skills For The Future Are Those Most at Risk

Perhaps most concerning of all, the skills we most need for the future are among those most at risk. A Boston Consulting Group study of senior executives found that judgment and decision-making, along with problem-framing, rank among the skills most vulnerable to erosion from AI. These are the very skills we need to decide when to trust AI in the first place!

Nor does experience protect us. In a study published in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology, experienced physicians' rate of spotting precancerous growths without AI dropped by about 20% within three months of starting to use it.

And technology can fail us when we least expect it. Prince Harry learned this on a public stage in September 2026, midway through a speech at the Clinton Global Initiative about the dangers of AI for young people. When his teleprompter failed, he was unable to continue and left the stage. Whoever wrote the speech, the lesson holds: if we haven't done the thinking up front, we have nothing to fall back on when the screen goes dark.

How to Decide What to Keep

We're at the early learning curve on the vast benefits of GenAI to humanity. Yet as we move up it, we must be increasingly intentional about what we outsource and what we keep doing ourselves. Before handing over a task, ask yourself three questions:

1. Does this skill matter to how I connect, influence, and live?

Some skills you can let go of without much loss. My children will pay little price for not knowing their times tables by heart as I did. But framing the right question, finding the right words in a hard conversation, or making a tough call when there's no obvious answer are skills worth protecting, even when we feel pressure to move faster.

2. Could I explain, defend, or correct what AI produces?

AI can make our work look smarter than our thinking actually is. A polished slide deck is easy to produce. Defending it when someone asks about bullet point is another matter. If you can't explain its reasoning, stay more involved, not less.

3. What capacity might I lose if I stop doing this myself?

Like skipping the gym, one shortcut is no big deal. Scale it over a thousand, and the muscle weakens. Weigh the time you save today against the capacity you might lose tomorrow.

Choosing effort over convenience is rarely rewarded in the short term. Writing the email yourself or wrestling with a problem before asking the chatbot can feel like a waste of time when a faster option is right there. But every choice shapes the future, often in ways we cannot see in the moment we decide.

Rethink Mental Effort as an Investment, Not a Cost

That extra mental effort builds (and protects) both the inner confidence and the capability that no algorithm can replace. It's what lets us sit with the discomfort of the "messy middle" rather than racing for false certainties, and discern the wiser path when repairing trust with someone we care about or addressing tension in our team. As the world grows faster and messier, and AI grows more capable, these human capacities will only become more valuable.

To be clear, I used AI to proofread this article and substantiate research to support my core premise. But I didn't use AI to write it. Not that I'm immune to the temptation. Rather, I know that outsourcing my writing to AI risks gradually reducing my ability to write anything worth reading.

The same is true for us all - every shortcut we take casts a small vote for the brain, and the person, we will become tomorrow.

item.title: Why Quality Beats Quantity When It Comes to Life and Living
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Why Quality Beats Quantity When It Comes to Life and Living

Beyond longevity, we can seek sustainable hybrid flourishing.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Recent global research shows that longer lifespan has not produced matching gains in healthy longevity.
  • A serious longevity agenda asks how to cultivate not growth but flourishing across the whole life cycle.
  • With the rise of generative AI, lifelong learning is no longer optional; it is becoming indispensable.
Meaningful longevity involves preserving the conditions that make life worth extending, not because of but amid technological assets.
Source: Walther, AI-generated with ChatGPT / OpenAI, 2026

For most of human history, longevity was a simple ambition. More years meant victory over hunger, infection, injury, and early death. Now the question has sharpened: If we add years, what kind of life, and what kind of world, receives them? Recent global research shows, however, that longer lifespan has not produced matching gains in healthy longevity everywhere. Even healthspan draws too small a circle.

Extra years can have uneven consequences, within a single person. Extra years may bring freedom and contribution, or insecurity and dependence. A person can reach 90 with a sound heart and strong legs while living inside a fragmented society, an unaffordable economy, a destabilized climate, and a technological environment that has eroded the appetite to think, question, and choose. That person has become a spectator in a life steered by devices. A serious longevity agenda looks beyond quantity to quality, asking how to cultivate not growth but flourishing across the whole life cycle. Moving forward, the quest for meaningful longevity must mean preserving the conditions that make life worth extending, not because of but amid technological assets.

A longer life rewrites the architecture of living

By 2030, one in six people worldwide will be aged 60 or older; by 2050, the 60-plus population is expected to reach 2.1 billion. Families, work, care, and education all reshuffle. The old sequence of learn, work, and retire belongs to another era. A century-long life may hold several careers, repeated study, caregiving, reinvention, and recovery. Healthy-longevity investment can reduce disease and disability while supporting productivity and participation. Education must not be limited to the period of youth, purpose is not confined to employment, and aging cannot sensibly be treated as a long epilogue. This has always been possible—but with the rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI), lifelong learning is no longer optional; it is becoming indispensable.

There is no meaningful longevity on an unhealthy planet.

Population health begins with planetary health. Air, water, food, temperature, and biodiversity are ingredients of a healthy body. Healthy aging itself is strongly influenced by physical and social environments. Climate disruption compounds heat exposure, disease risk, food insecurity, and displacement, and older people often stand among the most exposed. The investment logic is hard to defend. Developing countries face adaptation needs of roughly U.S.$310-365 billion annually by 2035, while international public adaptation finance reached only U.S.$26 billion in 2023. Capital meanwhile floods the digital economy, where investment is highly concentrated. AI can extend healthcare, sharpen resource use, and strengthen resilience. Yet a civilization that drains soil, water, climate stability, and human capability while stacking up computational power is growing poorer in every durable sense. It swaps foundational wealth for artificial capacity and mails the bill to the future.

The invisible longevity risk: agency decay

That bill arrives in cognitive currency, too. Generative AI can widen access to knowledge, creativity, and productivity. It can also make skipping the thinking wonderfully convenient. A 2025 study found that greater confidence in AI went with less critical-thinking effort, while greater confidence in one’s own ability went with more. The danger accumulates in tiny substitutions: We stop calculating, then navigating, remembering, drafting, analyzing, and eventually judging, because something else does each task faster. Assistance hardens into habit, habit slides into dependence, and dependence narrows agency.

For longer-lived societies, cognitive passivity would be a peculiar kind of progress. Twenty additional years offer thin flourishing to people who lose the capability or desire to author them. Human agency, our capacity to perceive alternatives, reason, imagine, decide, and act, deserves a seat beside physical and mental health as a core dimension of longevity.

Lifelong learning for a hybrid century

Here longevity turns into opportunity. Lifelong learning can serve as the infrastructure for hybrid intelligence: strengthening and combining natural and artificial intelligence while each keeps its own role. Technology literacy helps us understand and use capable systems; human literacy keeps critical thought, imagination, values, and judgment awake. Both perish without use.

Our generation holds a singular position. We may be the last analogue generation: old enough to remember ordinary life before algorithms mediated so much communication, knowledge, and choice; young enough to help build what follows. We remember navigating without a device, wrestling with unanswered questions, creating before prompting. We also feel AI’s possibilities. The social architecture we build now will influence whether our children, and our older selves, flourish with technology or slowly languish beneath it.

Four conditions for hybrid flourishing

A longer hybrid life rests on four mutually reinforcing capacities.

First, lifelong learning: renewing, again, our ability to understand, contribute, and cultivate hybrid intelligence.

Second, living intelligently with uncertainty: A child born today may see the 22nd century, and agency will serve that child better than prediction.

Third, systemic understanding: Society, economy, ecology, and technology keep reshaping one another, so solutions that optimize one domain by exporting costs to another rarely endure.

Fourth, hybrid flourishing starts from the inside out and is nurtured from the outside in: Agency cannot replace clean air, education, healthcare, security, working institutions, social connection, or technology that augments human capability. Flourishing emerges from the interplay of inner capacity and external conditions, and each can strengthen or diminish the other.

What are we using the extra years for?

Longevity hands humanity more time. AI promises to save it. Economic systems price it. Digital platforms compete for it. Climate change reminds us that it can run out. The central challenge of a longer hybrid life may be deciding what deserves our time.

We can use natural and artificial intelligence to extract more from finite systems and accelerate whatever pays fastest. We can also use longer lives to lengthen our horizon: learning repeatedly, restoring what we have depleted, thinking independently, contributing across generations, and designing technologies that enlarge human possibility. The defining achievement of longevity will be the quality of the added years: whether they remain recognisably ours, and whether the world inherited by those who follow still gives them room to flourish.

Let’s learn anew—or for the first time—to treat life as a precious, beautiful resource. Longevity measures how consciously, capably, and generously we live, at every age, no matter where we live.

item.title: Why We Test the People We Love
item.description:
Relationships

Why We Test the People We Love

What indirect reassurance-seeking reveals about your personality.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Testing the people we love often reflects emotional sensitivity rather than a desire to manipulate.
  • Testing can backfire by creating the very distance or conflict it was designed to detect.
  • Small, direct expressions of need tend to build more trust over time than indirect tests do.

One of my clients, Jess, came into a session frustrated with her partner. She had been feeling overwhelmed with work and he hadn't offered to help around the house. She hadn't asked, but she reasoned that he should have known because her stress was so obvious. By the end of the week, she felt her anger growing and told her partner she needed space.

This is a test. Although Jess wasn't aware that she was testing her partner, she was trying to find out whether she could count on him.

Why People Test Those Closest to Them

Testing behaviors in relationships are easy to miss because the person giving them often doesn't recognize that's what they're doing. Tests can look like dropping a hint to see if the other person picks up on it, going quiet and waiting, or picking a small argument to see if the other person will stay.

The real question underlying these tests is almost always: Is this relationship safe? Do I actually matter here?

At its most basic level, it's completely reasonable to want to know where you stand in a relationship. And when the people in your life respond in a way you've determined means they care, you experience relief.

At the same time, a failed test and a missed cue can look exactly the same. In Jess' situation, her partner failing to spontaneously offer help could be because he didn't care, or because she didn't ask for it and he didn't want to overstep.

The Personality Connection

Testing behaviors tend to show up more in people who score lower on the trust dimension of agreeableness, one of the Big Five traits that reflects how cooperative and trusting someone tends to be in relationships.

But lower trust doesn't appear from nowhere. For many people, it developed in earlier relationships where expressing needs directly either went unmet or made things worse. If asking for help as a child meant being told you were too needy, or being honest about what you wanted in a past relationship led to conflict or rejection, indirect communication becomes a reasonable adaptation. Hinting, testing, and pulling back are strategies that developed in an environment where the direct version wasn't safe.

The problem is that those strategies follow people into relationships where the rules are different. A partner who would respond warmly to a direct request never gets the chance, because the request never comes in a form they can recognize and respond to.

Why the Test Backfires

When one partner pulls back to see what the other will do, the other partner often senses something is off and pulls back too. Research suggests that indirect bids for reassurance tend to increase relationship anxiety over time rather than reduce it. The test is designed to answer the question, "Can I count on you?" However, because it's indirect, the answer it produces is almost always ambiguous. Ambiguity in a relationship tends to feed more emotional sensitivity, not less.

This can become a cycle. More uncertainty leads to more testing and more missed signals, which creates more distance and more doubt.

What to Try Instead

This isn't about becoming fully transparent overnight. It's about running a small experiment.

Pick one thing you would normally hint at or leave unasked, and ask for it directly. Not a test of the relationship, just a request. Notice what actually happens. You may find, as my clients often do, that the anticipation of asking was significantly worse than the actual asking.

Those small experiments build a different kind of evidence: accumulated proof that asking directly is usually survivable, and that the people worth keeping close tend to show up when asked. Over time, the trail of evidence rewrites the prediction. The personality dial doesn't shift in a single conversation, but it shifts, and the relationship shifts with it.

item.title: Men Cry for This One Reason
item.description:
Gender

Men Cry for This One Reason

Few social contexts "permit" men to cry openly.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Men cry between 5 and 17 times a year on average versus between 30 and 64 times a year for women.
  • Crying has less to do with sex differences and more to do with social norms.
  • Men accepting of feminine norms cried more often and were more likely to view crying as beneficial.

In a country where masculinity is prized, it’s rare to see a man cry. I remember my dad crying only once during my childhood. On television, for instance, alpha male Don Draper (played by Jon Hamm) broke down in tears only twice during the entire run of "Mad Men"—once when his closest confidante Anna Draper died of cancer and once in group therapy when he realized how destructive he was to those who loved him.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) cites research that men cry between 5 and 17 times a year on average compared with between 30 and 64 times a year for women. Honestly, these numbers seem a bit high to me, but this gives you an idea that men cry infrequently—except for in one specific situation.

Social acceptance

A cross-cultural survey including 893 respondents from Australia, Croatia, the Netherlands, Thailand, and the United Kingdom examined how gender, gender roles, and beliefs about crying varied by culture.

Intriguingly, results were consistent across cultures.

Source: Daniel Reche / Pexels

Women reported crying more frequently and intensely than men did, which was supported by prior research. Internalized gender roles played a large role in whether men cry, with the mentality that “Boys don’t cry” entrenched in many societies.

Study participants who aligned with more traditional, masculine gender roles cried less and perceived crying as being less helpful. Men accepting of feminine norms cried more and were more likely to perceive crying as beneficial.

These beliefs also predicted whether crying resulted in emotional relief. Participants who believed crying was helpful were more likely to report relief following a period of crying.

Another important finding from the study was that crying functioned as a social signal. When crying among familiar others, these people were consoled by their supportive responses.

Overall, the findings suggest that crying has less to do with sex differences and more to do with norms, personal beliefs, and social dynamics.

The authors wrote: “When a crier said that they were helped by either instrumental, informational, or physical means, they tended to report a better emotional state following crying than those who did not receive help, but who were around at least one other person.”

The authors were careful to say that the presence of others has a complex relationship with how people evaluate their emotional state after crying. Furthermore, the country of origin may also influence such feelings.

When men do cry

Certain contexts permit men to cry more freely without being socially penalized—including sports competitions. Male athletes often cry after major losses or defeats.

article continues after advertisement

But even in these contexts, social norms play a role. In a study published in Frontiers in Psychology, participants viewed men who cried after losing a weightlifting competition as more masculine than men who cried after losing a figure skating competition. Similarly, a crying male nurse was viewed as less emotionally appropriate, less emotionally strong, and lower in workplace status than a crying male firefighter.

“Taken together, these findings suggest that men who are perceived to embody cultural ideals of masculinity may be given more room to cry than those who are perceived as less stereotypically masculine,” the authors concluded.

This study was limited by examining only “sad crying.” Little is known about joyous, fearful, or angry crying.

On a related note, we’ve all seen that even at funerals some men don’t cry, which could reflect social norms about crying.

item.title: Love: The Ultimate and Highest Goal
item.description:
Relationships

Love: The Ultimate and Highest Goal

Love offers great insight into the human quest for meaning.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Love has many definitions and applications in concept and practice.
  • Love offers great insight into the human quest for meaning.
  • Love involves extending beyond oneself and caring about the highest good of others.
Source: Rosy/Bad Homburg/Germany/Pixabay

We are living in a very uncertain and turbulent time, one characterized in many places around the world by unbridled anger, conflict, division, intolerance, and outright hate. Against such a fragile and highly sensitive backdrop, I believe that it is a good time to reflect upon and discuss the relationship between “love” and the human quest for meaning.

Viktor Frankl’s Perspective on Love and Meaning

In this regard, the world-renowned psychiatrist, existential philosopher, and Holocaust survivor Viktor E. Frankl’s holistic view on the importance of our intuitive capacity for love offers great insight into how meaning in everyday life—and even at work—reveals itself.

“Love is the ultimate and the highest goal to which man can aspire.... The salvation of man is through love and in love. I understood how a man who has nothing left in this world still may know bliss, be it only for a brief moment, in the contemplation of his beloved.”

Frankl wrote these words in his classic bestseller, Man’s Search for Meaning,1 a book that was first published in German in 1946 under the title, “Ein Psycholog erlebt das Konzentrationslager” (From Death-Camp to Existentialism). For good reason, Man's Search for Meaning remains one of the most important books of modern times (the Library of Congress named it one of the 10 most influential books in America). Indeed, Frankl’s personal story of finding a reason to live in the most horrendous of circumstances—Nazi concentration camps—has inspired millions of people around the world. I am both honored and humbled to have had him as a mentor.

Alex Pattakos with Viktor Frankl at his home, Vienna, Austria, August 1996
Source: Alex Pattakos

It is against this personal backdrop that Frankl’s quote about love must be considered. And considered very seriously. You see, although Frankl was blessed with surviving his horrific ordeal in four different Nazi death camps, his mother, father, wife, and brother were not so fortunate.

And even though he had been stripped of everything, down—literally—to the bare bones of his humanity, Frankl experienced moments of bliss, especially when he thought of those he loved—his wife, parents, brother, and others who were dear to him. In no uncertain terms, he learned unequivocally that love was his salvation and that, among all the values that offered him a source of personal meaning, it was love that proved to be the “ultimate and highest goal to which he could aspire.”

article continues after advertisement

I would like all of us to reflect seriously upon the above passage from Man's Search for Meaning, along with Frankl’s personal, love-affirming experience, today, tomorrow, and forever. What do you think about it? How does it make you feel? How and in what ways are you bringing and weaving love into your life? Into your work?

Into your “work"?! Yes, that is what I said. Even though we don’t normally associate this particular “L” word with work or the workplace, it does have an important and meaningful role to play.

Love in the Workplace

I’m not talking about romantic love, even though we all know that it sometimes finds its way into the work setting. I’m talking about love in the sense of caring about another person’s “highest good.” And this includes those with whom we may work, such as co-workers, colleagues, associates, customers, vendors, partners, students, patients, and so on.

This notion of work and the workplace is not as far-fetched as one might initially think. For instance, in our book, Prisoners of Our Thoughts,2 we introduce a company, Skaltek, a major equipment manufacturer based in Stockholm, Sweden, where the task of building a meaningful workplace is taken very seriously. In this connection, consider the words of Őystein Skalleberg, the founder of Skaltek, as he describes his philosophy about people and work:

“Every human being is a Leonardo da Vinci. The only problem is that he doesn't know it. His parents didn't know it, and they didn’t treat him like a Leonardo. Therefore, he didn't become like a Leonardo. That's my basic theory.”

Because Skalleberg sought to practice what he preached, there are many attributes of the working environment at Skaltek that would be considered “radical” by even some of the most innovative companies/organizations in the private and public sectors in the world today. One is an annual employment appraisal process that involves the use of randomly selected performance review teams. According to Skalleberg, since no one knows who will be conducting their performance review each year, “Everybody smiles in all directions!”

article continues after advertisement

Skalleberg also has a revolutionary formula for building a company culture in the postmodern era:

Confidence is the start of it,
Joy is a part of it,
Love is the heart of it.

Doesn’t Skaltek sound like a company with an inspirational and aspirational meaning-focused philosophy about bringing love to work? Why not make now the time to (re)affirm too that “love is the ultimate and highest goal” to which we all can aspire in life, work, and society?

A version of this post also appears on The Huffington Post.

item.title: Has Medicine Forgotten How to Read?
item.description:
Cognition

Has Medicine Forgotten How to Read?

Before it was a science of language, semiotics was the science of symptoms.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Semiotics, the study of signs, belonged to medicine before it passed to linguists.
  • AI and algorithms can map a finding to a disease but ignore what the finding means for the patient.
  • Semiotics offers medicine a framework for understanding the context of data.

By Prav Prathapan, Senior Medical Writer, Encephalitis International.

Source: Shuttermon via iStock

A year after herpes simplex encephalitis, a woman returns for her follow-up MRI. The scan is thankfully clean. The report says no evidence of active disease, and it’s correct.

Yet her husband, sitting beside her, says she has not come back the same person.

Only one of these findings gets to be recorded, and determines what happens next. The other one leaves the room with them.

This is not a failure of scanning. It is a failure of reading, and medicine used to have a discipline for it.

Ancient origins

Long before ‘semiotics’ belonged to linguists and literary theorists, it belonged to physicians.

The word comes from the Greek sēmeion, ‘sign’, and medical semiotics was the medical speciality of reading the body (1); of interpreting the signs and symptoms through which a disease presents itself.

The roots of medical semiotics extend to Hippocrates (c. 460–c. 370 BCE), whose treatises on prognosis taught physicians to gather signs (the colour of the skin, the features of the breath, the pattern of a fever, etc.) and to infer from them the course of an illness.

Taught, then forgotten

For centuries, semiotics held a fixed place in the European medical curriculum. In the German-speaking world, students learned Semiotik (2) and in Italy, semeiotica medica was a named chair and discipline well into the twentieth century (3).

Then it faded. There is now a ‘total absence of medical semiotics in the curriculum of medical schools in the English-speaking world’ (4). One of the main reasons for this: as laboratory tests, biochemistry, and imaging techniques matured, diagnosis was outsourced from the bedside to the machine.

The AI medical world

Today, the story is thrown into even sharper relief with deep-learning systems able to perform the pattern recognition traditionally done by the trained physician.

So what’s the problem? It’s the need for clarity. Semiotics helps us see what the machine does well and where it falls short.

A sign, as philosopher and logician Charles Peirce (1839–1914) defined it, has at least three parts: a ‘representamen’ (the finding), the ‘object’ it points to (the disease), and the ‘interpretant’ (what it means for someone).

An algorithm is terrific at the first two: mapping the finding to the disease across millions of cases. The difficulty is the last one.

For Peirce, semiosis, the process by which signs emerge, is unlimited: every interpretant becomes a sign in its turn, calling for interpretation of its own.

The AI’s chain closes when it arrives at a label. In the consulting room, that is where the chain is supposed to open up. When a machine says ‘No evidence of active disease’, it could mean relief, confusion, or, for a woman a year out from encephalitis, the question of why the good news fails to describe her life.

The AI sees a conclusion. She sees a premise.

So what do we do?

Renewing medical semiotics is not a retreat from the digital. It is a way of dividing the labour (and the thinking) better. Here are some things for the clinician to keep in mind:

  • Treat the machine as a producer of signs, not verdicts.
  • Give the interpretant somewhere to live in the record. If the note holds only findings, the context meaning isn’t passed to other clinicians.
  • Record the broader story. Note what the patient and their families understand the results to mean and what they take to have changed (5).
  • Use the infrastructure that already exists. Rita Charon’s narrative medicine trains exactly the capacity the algorithm lacks: ‘the ability to acknowledge, absorb, interpret, and act on the stories and plights of others’ (6). It has a literature and a curriculum.

As machines absorb more of the sign-to-object mapping, the distinctly human task does not vanish; it concentrates and moves towards the interpretant.

The scan was right. The report was right. Both were faithful answers to a question nobody in that room was asking. A medicine that can tell the difference between measurement and meaning is a better medicine.

item.title: How to Protect Yourself Against AI-Powered Disinformation
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

How to Protect Yourself Against AI-Powered Disinformation

Propaganda now is decentralized, deliberately contradictory, and personalized.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • New reports reveal that Russia has been actively interfering in the U.S. midterm elections for months.
  • Question who benefits if you share posts, pause before reposting, and read sources outside your bubble.
  • Due to constant exposure to Russian disinformation, Ukraine's civil society has developed a robust response.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is driving new ways to manipulate democracy. And this election season, it’s coming to a smartphone screen near you.

New intelligence reports show that over the past several months, Russia has again embarked on a campaign to meddle in American elections.

In the run-up to the 2026 midterms, the New York Times reports that the U.S. intelligence community has been monitoring social media campaigns and AI-powered deepfake videos depicting Hollywood celebrities such as Julia Roberts or Jamie Lee Curtis criticizing Democratic candidates.

One of the deepfakes even depicted actress Sarah Jessica Parker calling both Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Democratic candidates “Nazis.”

These videos use lies to amplify typical attack lines against candidates’ positions on immigration and LGBT rights, along with accusations of corruption and antisemitism.

The assessments also point to Iran using similar tactics to disrupt U.S. democracy.

Because Russia is distracted by its grueling war against Ukraine, experts believe this year’s manipulation during the U.S. midterms is relatively minor compared with Russia’s massive influence operation during the 2016 presidential election.

Disinformation and propaganda efforts have long been part of Russia’s foreign policy and cognitive warfare strategy. They have exploited critical vulnerabilities in free societies through the 2016 election, the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, and more recently during its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. These techniques have been deployed throughout the world, including in recent elections in Georgia and Moldova, and upcoming contests in Germany, France, and Estonia.

Understanding how such strategies work is essential to being a savvy consumer of modern media, especially in the social media and AI era.

New Era of Propaganda

During World War II, propaganda worked differently. In Germany, the Nazi Party’s chief propagandist Josef Goebbels executed a top-down strategy. With total command of broadcasters and mass media, Goebbels dictated the truth through radio, film reels, and posters.

In today’s fractured and high-speed information landscape, authoritarian information manipulators use different techniques to reach similar outcomes, says Halyna Padalko, a postdoctoral scholar at MIT from Ukraine. She studies disinformation and teaches courses on modern propaganda techniques.

article continues after advertisement

Modern propaganda is decentralized, rather than centralized. Instead of a singular ministry, there are armies of state media outlets, private contractors, social media influencers, and automated bot networks.

Next, techniques practiced by Russia are not necessarily designed to induce a whole population to believe the same lie; rather, they aim to confuse enough of the population such that people stop believing what’s real. AI deepfakes only accelerate an already worrying trend.

Disinformation shatters the notion of a singular truth, rather than dictates it. Bot farms amplify a range of distorted narratives to the point that individuals quit believing it’s possible to know the truth, or are so overwhelmed they give up. Contradictory or inconsistent information makes it harder to act or can lead us into a state of passivity.

Finally, propaganda and disinformation are now highly personalized. Narratives and fake news can be algorithmically deployed to those most susceptible, based on the habits, tastes, preferences, and demographics of individual users. Because it stokes hate or fear, it triggers deep urgency in users to click or share it, and then it is further amplified when those posts trigger intense arguments.

“The goal is often not to convince people of a specific alternative fact but to exhaust their trust in the idea that truth is knowable at all,” Padalko said.

Protecting Yourself

Padalko recommends several tips for how individuals can inoculate themselves against disinformation.

A few practical habits can help you engage with discernment, keep your distance, and ultimately be part of the solution.

First, check the source's incentive, not just its claim. Ask yourself: Who benefits if I believe this? A story engineered to make you angry, afraid, or triumphant is worth extra scrutiny. Strong emotion is often the point, not a side effect. If it confirms your existing viewpoint, that could be as manipulative. Terms such as “regime,” “liberators,” or “so-called” work to polarize readers toward one side or to call facts into question.

Next, slow down before sharing. Pause and consider. Disinformation is designed to spread far faster than fact-checkers can respond. Make sure to read the story, check who wrote it, and determine whether independent outlets are reporting similar information. Doing this usually filters out a large percentage of manipulated content.

Take special care that sources confirming a piece of information are indeed independent. “Volume is not evidence,” Padalko said. “Ten accounts repeating the same claims can still be one source amplified by bots.”

Be aware of short viral video clips that purport to show a slanted viewpoint: Recycled or out-of-context imagery is one of the most common tricks.

article continues after advertisement

Finally, diversify and design your media diet so that you don’t strictly read outlets that share your viewpoint. This helps you notice when a story online appears in a particular ideological echo chamber.

A Society Fights Back

Over the past two decades, including years of full-scale war, Ukraine has borne the brunt of Russian disinformation campaigns.

As a matter of survival, the nation has responded by building a whole-of-society inoculation system, pairing government coordination with private-sector AI tools, independent watchdogs, and mass civic education.

National polls show that the share of Ukrainians with “above average” media literacy increased from 55 percent in 2021 to 81 percent in 2022, just as Russia’s full-scale invasion launched.

The Ministry of Culture's "Filter" project runs nationwide campaigns teaching people to spot deepfakes and manipulated narratives. The government’s Diia.Education platform streams media-literacy content to more than two million users. And Ukraine’s tech community regularly organizes hackathons that bring together teams to prototype disinformation detectors in 72-hour sprints.

Much of the success of Ukraine’s model stems from how it engages civil society: Homegrown AI companies work directly with stratcom units within the government, coordinating detection efforts, forecasting how false narratives will spread across dozens of countries, mapping bot-driven coordination, or monitoring Russian Telegram channels for emerging propaganda themes.

At the same time, independent journalists perform in-depth investigations, and millions of citizens play their role flagging and verifying questionable content in real time.

“That redundancy is what has let Ukraine keep pace with and sometimes get ahead of a Russian propaganda machine that is built for volume and speed,” Padalko said.

item.title: An Optimistic View of the Future of Work
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

An Optimistic View of the Future of Work

The key is to design an economic metric, the labor transition cushion.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • AI is the bulldozer for the mind, letting one person accomplish what once required entire teams.
  • The real danger is transition speed: displacement could outrun reskilling, weakening jobs and demand.
  • Like past technologies, AI won’t end work; it will redefine roles and expand what is worth creating.

My favorite analogy for the future of work: Years ago, a hundred men with shovels would dig a trench, slowly, methodically, their labor measured in sweat and hours. Then came the bulldozer. Inevitably, a group of ditch diggers must have sat together, shaking their heads, lamenting that this infernal machine would take all their jobs. And in a narrow sense, they were right. The bulldozer did replace them. But that framing, while emotionally poignant, was economically incomplete. The bulldozer redefined the unit of labor itself: A single operator could now do the work of a hundred humans.

Bulldozers for the Mi
Source: Moses Ma

The key learning is that the outcome was not a world with 99 unemployed workers lingering at the margins of society. Instead, something more interesting happened. Entirely new roles emerged around the machine—operators, mechanics, planners, supervisors, automotive engineers and designers, bulldozer salesmen—and more importantly, the cost of excavation collapsed. And when something becomes cheaper, humans in a society don’t simply do less of it with fewer people; we start doing dramatically more of it. Roads stretched farther, cities expanded faster, infrastructure projects that once seemed uneconomical suddenly became viable. The bulldozer didn’t eliminate work; it expanded the frontier of what was worth building. Productivity, in this sense, doesn’t shrink the economy—it enlarges it.

Now we are living through a similar moment, except the bulldozer has moved from the physical world into the cognitive one. AI is not a better shovel; it is a bulldozer for the mind. It compresses activities that once took days into minutes—coding, design, analysis, synthesis, writing, planning—and allows a single individual to produce at a scale previously reserved for teams. And so, predictably, the same fear returns.

A recent paper, The AI Layoff Trap by Brett Hemenway Falk and Gerry Tsoukalas, articulates the systemic risk with unusual clarity. As they write, “If AI displaces human workers faster than the economy can reabsorb them, it risks eroding the very consumer demand firms depend on.” This is the core paradox. Companies automate to reduce costs and increase efficiency, but in doing so, they may undercut the income base of the very consumers who sustain demand. The problem compounds because no individual firm can afford to opt out. As the authors note, “demand externalities trap rational firms,” creating a dynamic where each company, acting logically in isolation, contributes to a collectively suboptimal outcome. We are not facing a failure of intelligence or intent, but a coordination failure embedded in the system's structure itself.

The risk, then, is not that AI will replace work—that is inevitable—but that it will do so faster than society can metabolize the change. This creates what might be called a bridge problem. We are crossing from one economic paradigm to another, from a system where labor income drives consumption and growth, to one where AI-driven productivity becomes the dominant force. But the bridge between these worlds is narrow and unstable. If too many people try to cross at once—if displacement outpaces reintegration—the result is not a smooth transition but an avalanche. The issue is not the destination, but that crossing into the future. The key is to build a stronger bridge, an economic metric or a labor transition cushion.

The solution, then, is not to slow down the adoption of the bulldozer. History suggests that attempts to halt technological progress are both futile and counterproductive. Instead, the focus can shift to building the infrastructure, and people can learn how to operate that new technology and be productive within the new system. In practical terms, this means universal, continuous, and affordable AI reskilling—not as a one-time intervention, but as a persistent layer of the economy, as fundamental as education or transportation. The constraint is no longer raw intelligence; it is fluency in collaborating with increasingly powerful systems.

If we get this right, the story unfolds much as it did before. The ditch diggers do not disappear; they evolve. They become operators, orchestrators, designers of systems that move far more earth—literal or metaphorical—than ever before. One may have a dream of becoming an architect; dedication and sheer will make it happen.

And the economy, rather than contracting under the weight of automation, expands into new domains of possibility. The bulldozer does not end work. It changes its shape and scope, eventually expanding the imagination of what is possible for someone with a dream, or all of humanity.

item.title: Do You Know What You Want—or Just What You Want to Avoid?
item.description:
Motivation

Do You Know What You Want—or Just What You Want to Avoid?

Why solving problems isn’t the same as building a better life.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Many goals describe what we want to stop, not what we want to create.
  • Longitudinal research links avoidance goals with more stress and poorer well-being.
  • Reducing anxiety, conflict, or failure is not the same as cultivating courage, intimacy, or mastery.

"I want to stop feeling so behind."

"I want to stop overthinking social interactions."

"I want to stop having the same arguments with my partner."

These sound like goals. But none of them actually express what you want. They only describe what you want to stop.

That matters because the direction of our lives is shaped by the goals we pursue. If those goals are defined only by what we want to escape, we can spend years solving problems and still be no closer to the life we actually want.

The Problem–Remedy–Outcome (PRO) model offers a useful framework to separate what we want to stop from what we actually want to create (Tompkins & Lawley, 2006):

  • Problem: Something exists that you do not want. “I feel overwhelmed.”
  • Remedy: You want the problem gone. “I want to stop feeling overwhelmed.”
  • Outcome: You describe what you actually want to exist instead. “I want to feel calm and able to choose what I focus on.”

Problem and Remedy are organised around the problem, whereas Outcome builds toward the desired state. Take insecurity for example:

  1. “I feel insecure.” → Problem
  2. “I want to be less insecure.” → Remedy
  3. “I want more confidence.” → a starting Outcome
  4. “I want to be able to walk into a room, approach people I'm interested in, and speak freely even if I'm nervous.” → a much richer Outcome

This changes how we think about change

You might want to spend less time on your phone, which sounds like a goal. But it only says what should disappear, not what should take its place.

Without something compelling to take its place, removing the behaviour leaves a vacuum—and old habits have an easy way back in.

By shifting to the ideal outcome—“I want evenings filled with things absorbing enough that I forget to check my phone”—you now have something concrete to build toward.

So, whenever you notice yourself saying:

  • “I need to stop…”
  • “I need to be less…”
  • “I want to get rid of…”

ask one additional question:

“And if that were no longer the problem, what would I want to be happening instead?”

Keep going until the answer describes something you could actually move toward.

Helping someone find their own outcome

PRO emerged from the Clean Language method of questioning, which explores someone’s experience while minimising the assumptions and interpretations introduced by the person asking the questions.

As a result, instead of shaping someone’s answer, Clean Language helps them articulate their own (Tompkins & Lawley, 2006). For example:

Person: “I’m exhausted.” (Problem)

Facilitator: “And when you’re exhausted, what would you like to have happen?”

Person: “I need to stop working so much.” (Remedy)

Facilitator: “And when you stop working so much, what would you like to happen?”

Person: “I want enough energy after work to enjoy time with my family.” (Outcome)

This shifts the attention while preserving the personal growth that comes from constructing one’s own outcome.

Clear outcomes create more options

Compare “I want to stop feeling anxious” with “I want to be able to speak freely in meetings even when some anxiety is present.”

The second opens up far more possibilities. And crucially, the outcome does not require the problem to disappear first.

Instead of designing your life entirely in reaction to what is wrong with it, you can ask a more expansive question:

Not “What needs to disappear?” but “What needs to exist?”

A good life is more than the absence of bad things

Across several areas of psychology, reducing the negative is not the same as cultivating the positive:

  • No anxiety ≠ courage.
  • No conflict ≠ intimacy.
  • No failure ≠ mastery.

This idea was central to the emergence of positive psychology. Martin Seligman and Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi argued that psychology should concern itself not only with pathology and weakness but also with strengths and positive functioning (Seligman & Csikszentmihalyi, 2000):

“Treatment is not just fixing what is broken; it is nurturing what is best.”

A similar distinction is made between “approach goals” and “avoidance goals”:

  • Approach goals: moving toward a desired state.
  • Avoidance goals: preventing or escaping an undesired state.

Longitudinal research has found that avoidance goals can predict greater stress, more reliance on avoidant coping, and poorer subjective well-being (Elliot et al., 2011).

This does not mean avoidance is always wrong. Sometimes preventing or escaping an undesired state is precisely the right focus (e.g., in an abusive relationship). The aim is not to ignore the problem or the remedy but to move beyond them toward a clearly defined outcome.

So, whenever you find yourself wanting less of something, ask:

“What do I want more of instead?”

Not: “I want less stress.”
But: “I want more time, control, and freedom in my week.”

Not: “I want to stop being insecure.”
But: “I want to become someone who can express what I think without constantly checking how it will be received.”

Not: “I want to stop feeling lonely.”
But: “I want to foster relationships in which I feel understood, valued, and connected.”

Then, we can build a life that reflects what we actually value—not merely what we’re trying to avoid.

item.title: A Secret Cause and Cure for Social Anxiety
item.description:
Shyness

A Secret Cause and Cure for Social Anxiety

Why the room feels harder for you than it seems to be for everyone else.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Many socially anxious people carry a buried sense that they are missing something inside.
  • The thing that’s actually missing is a full connection to their own emotions.
  • It feels like a flaw, but it’s just a feeling, and it often traces back to emotional neglect.
Source: New Africa / AdobeStock

"We're invited to the neighborhood barbecue!" Donald's wife Barbara says excitedly to him. They just moved into the area, and she is happy about the opportunity to meet their new neighbors. "Oh, that's nice, honey," Donald says back. But in fact, he is cringing inside. Secretly, he is making a plan to schedule a long meeting at work that afternoon so he will not have to attend.

Do you recognize something of yourself in Donald? Have you ever built a small, quiet excuse to avoid a room full of people?

In my psychology practice, I spent years with people who did exactly that, and almost none of them could tell me why. They were warm. They were liked. And they walked into gatherings certain, in some deep, unnameable way inside themselves, that they were the only person there who did not belong.

There is a name for what they were carrying. I call it the fatal flaw, and it is a deeply buried sense that:

Something is wrong with me. I am missing some vital ingredient that other people have. I am set apart, different. I don't quite fit in anywhere.

Fortunately, the fatal flaw is not as bad as it sounds, because it's not a real flaw. Instead, it's something far more powerful than a flaw. It's a feeling.

Legions of people walk this earth held back by something they cannot understand and for which they have no words. It's a feeling with the power to hold brilliant people back from achieving their full potential. It's a feeling that will not break you, but it will dog you. It will keep you standing alone at the PTA meeting, or sitting pretending to work while others chat freely at a conference. Unaddressed, it can set you apart so that you feel alone, and it can gradually wear away your connection to the world.

Where It Comes From

The fatal flaw is a product of an invisible, subtle, powerful force: childhood emotional neglect, a parent's failure to respond enough to a child's emotional needs.

Children who grow up in households where their feelings are ignored or discouraged push their emotions down and away to adapt. As adults, they lack access to their own feelings, which are a vital source of richness and connection in life. Deep down, they sense something missing in them that other people have. It's their emotions. These two results combine to form this unnameable sense of being different, of not fitting in, of being alone and out of place—a perfect breeding ground for social anxiety.

Because its source is essentially invisible, many people who grew up this way are completely unaware, and so many with the fatal flaw are completely unaware. It is, in fact, your lack of awareness that gives the fatal flaw so much power over you.

And please know, this is so often no one's fault. Many emotionally neglectful parents are doing their best, and many were raised in the very same way themselves.

Donald, Two Years Later

Barbara and Donald just walked into the Johnsons' anniversary party. They only know a few people there. Donald stands uncomfortably next to Barbara while she introduces herself to some guests. He fights the urge to excuse himself and flee the room. "I feel that I don't fit in here, but I know that it's not true," he thinks to himself. "It's not real; it's just a feeling. It's my fatal flaw." Donald takes a deep breath and puts out his hand because he knows that as soon as he puts warmth out there, it will flow back to him. And his fatal flaw will be neutralized for the remainder of this party.

Nothing about Donald's situation changed between those two parties. He did not become more interesting, or better at small talk, or more liked. The only thing that changed is that he knows what the feeling is; instead of letting it control him, he is taking control of it.

Four Things You Can Do

  1. Recognize that your social anxiety is not based on reality, but is actually only a feeling. You feel you don't belong, but it is not actually true. Don't give the feeling so much power.
  2. Notice it in the room, while it’s happening. It tends to arrive early and quietly, as the urge to check your phone or step outside for air. Naming it while you’re standing there is what keeps it from running the show, and it is what lets you tap into the rich source of connection and belongingness that other people enjoy.
  3. Tell someone close to you about your fatal flaw so that they can help you by reminding and supporting you in social situations.
  4. Prepare yourself before every social occasion. Close your eyes, and walk yourself through it in your mind. Imagine yourself at the gathering, behaving warmly and confidently. Remind yourself that you are worthy and that you matter.

It Is Only a Feeling

Repeat to yourself often the words that Donald used:

I feel that I don't fit in here, but I know that it's not true. It's not real; it's only a feeling. It's my fatal flaw.

item.title: 6 Ways You Can Ease Your Fears
item.description:
Fear

6 Ways You Can Ease Your Fears

Fears are treated differently based on whether they are rational or irrational.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • We experience fear when we encounter something dangerous or painful, or even just something new.
  • Many fears are rooted in incidents from the past.
  • If a fear is irrational, then it can be a good idea to overcome it in an imaginary way.
Source: People Images / Shutterstock

Fear can be a burden, but it can also be a lifesaver. After millions of years of evolution, our brains are engineered to experience fear when we encounter something dangerous, something painful, or even just something new.

Without this healthy protection, human beings might go around eating poisonous foods, walking into traffic, and trying to pet untamed animals—all without even thinking about the consequences. Fears that keep us from doing those things are what we call healthy fears.

The trouble is, many fears are not so healthy. If your fears are shaping your decisions in an unhelpful way, making you feel sick, or keeping you from doing good and positive things you want to do, you can deal with them so you can get on with the life you want to live.

The first step is asking, Is what I’m afraid of scary and dangerous? Or is it maybe just scary? If something is both, you can probably identify a way it’s a threat to your well-being. For example, walking along the edge of a cliff in flip-flops is both scary and dangerous—you feel fear because you could trip, fall, and get hurt.

But what if a situation is just scary? For example, walking into a new workplace might give you a feeling of fear almost as intense as you felt on the cliff. But it does not pose a danger to your health or well-being.

If your brain doesn’t sort fears into the ones that are dangerous and the ones that aren’t, you can help it learn the difference using some of the following effective techniques:

Trust Your Strengths

Know that you have tools and abilities you can use and control to deal with fears. In your life, you’ve overcome struggles, fears, and setbacks. You’ve suffered pain and survived. You’ve learned complicated things—maybe to ride a bike, to swim, or to drive a car—all scary experiences in the beginning. You’ve likely overcome fear many times—when you started a new job, moved to a new locale, or started a committed relationship. Every day you are becoming more experienced and skilled.

These strengths are your tools when you face your fears. If a situation scares you, stop and think about everything you’ve learned and overcome. You are competent to deal with problems, and you are smart enough to know when you need to ask for help. Trust that if you set out to overcome a fear, you will be successful.

Go Back to the Beginning

Many fears are rooted in incidents from the past. A child who was bitten by a dog, for example, may become afraid of all dogs. One way to help ease these fears is to go back to that scary memory and put it in perspective. This is something you can do with the help of your subconscious. Think back to the moment your fear started, then think about how much you’ve changed and learned since the event.

Imagine your current self (or even a wiser future version of you) standing beside you, explaining that this is just one bad moment (or one scary dog, in this example). Think about how you are going to get past the moment and be OK. Doing this multiple times can help take away the lasting fear tied to a bad memory.

Face It a Little at a Time

Our minds were trained over millions of years to react to new people, things, and experiences with fear. You become careful in new situations so you are less likely to be hurt. Your mind is equally programmed to stop being afraid once you get used to something new.

This is why someone who’s never walked on a rooftop, for example, would feel terrified the first time they climbed up and looked down at the world. But people who install roofs for a living unlearn a lot of that fear—some can get up on a roof and walk around almost as comfortably as if they were on the ground.

Part of getting over fears is experiencing circumstances multiple times without anything bad happening. I’ve had patients overcome fears of everything from swimming to snakes, from being called on in class to riding on public transportation, by exposing themselves to the thing they’re afraid of a little at a time, multiple times.

For example, if you’re afraid of snakes, you could start off by talking about snakes, then looking at photographs of snakes, and then looking at videos about snakes. Once you become more comfortable, you can go see a snake in person, or even pet a snake. There’s no rule that says you must overcome any fear all at once. You can take little steps and get more confident over time.

Make Fun of Your Fear

Imagine your fear is itty-bitty, or wearing a clown’s nose, or with an amusing voice. Whenever you make your fear less real in your imagination, it loses some of its power.

In the Harry Potter books and movies, for example, when a creature called a boggart takes the form of each student’s worst fear, they use the riddikulus spell to make it seem silly and less scary. One student uses the spell to imagine transforming a frightening vampire into a cute bunny with big teeth. Think about how you can knock your own fear down to size.

Rational or Imagined?

How can you tell if a fear is likely to occur in real life? First, quiet your mind and ask out loud, “Should I be afraid of this?” What is your subconscious telling you? What is your gut instinct?

You can also ask a trusted friend, family member, counselor, or doctor to talk it out with you. If the fear is rational, then think about how you can change the situation so you can feel safe. For instance, if you are worried someone might break into your house, you can make it a habit to check that all the doors are locked before you go to bed.

If you decide a fear is irrational, then it can be a good idea to overcome it in an imaginary way, because rational arguments may not help relieve irrational fears. For instance, if you are afraid a ghost might haunt you, you could imagine a guardian angel can protect you.

Ask for Help

Just like most things in life, fears come in all sizes and strengths—from the inkling you don’t like something all the way to fears that keep you from living a normal life. It’s OK—and healthy—to have some reasonable fears, and it’s within your power to deal with moderate fears.

But if your fears are taking up a great deal of your time and energy, disrupting your daily routine, or causing you to be unhappy and anxious much of the time, it’s time to ask for help.

You may benefit from having a counselor or doctor to guide you through options for therapy, hypnosis, calming techniques, lifestyle changes, or even medications (which a doctor can discuss with you if the other approaches have not helped).

Takeaway

Like all subjective experiences, fears are experienced in the mind. This means that your fears can be reduced or resolved once you learn how to control your mind better (LeDoux & Pine, 2016).

item.title: Jane Goodall's Core Values Reject Human Exceptionalism
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Jane Goodall's Core Values Reject Human Exceptionalism

A year after her death, reflections on Goodall's science and hope.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Jane Goodall stressed that empathy and kindness are not enemies of scientific rigor and there always is hope.
  • We should always treat every single living being with the compassion and reverence they deserve.
Jane and Marc, one of the last times they were together, March 2926.
Source: Marc Bekoff

By Marc Bekoff, Ph.D. and Carolyn Cott

On October 1, 2025, Dr. Jane Goodall passed away at the age of 91. In her 65 years of research, advocacy, and persistence, she reshaped our understanding of non-human animals and dismantled the longstanding myth of human exceptionalism and separateness.

Before she stepped into the dense canopy of Gombe Stream, Tanzania, in 1960, mainstream science treated non-human animals largely as stimulus-response, instinct-driven mechanisms. Before her work, ethology—the scientific study of animal behavior—dismissed the suggestion that animals have minds, emotions, and individuality as unscientific—the cardinal sin of anthropomorphism.

Goodall proved her critics wrong, not with hostility but with rigorous, decades-spanning evidence.

The research that shifted our lens on who we are and who other animals are

Goodall's scientific research permanently altered the artificial boundary between humans and the rest of the natural world. Her book The Chimpanzees of Gombe, published in 1986, remains a classic, and she wrote or coauthored many other books. Goodall also won many awards for her scientific and humanitarian work. Her significant contributions include, but are not limited to, these areas:

  • Making and using tools by nonhumans: In November 1960, she observed David Greybeard (one of her named chimpanzees) stripping leaves off a twig to "fish" for termites, shattering the long-held belief that humans alone made and used tools. People didn't believe her until she showed them a video. The discovery prompted her mentor, Louis Leakey, to cable his now-famous line to Jane: "Now we must redefine tool, redefine Man, or accept chimpanzees as humans."
  • Changing the emotional landscape: Goodall documented deep maternal bonds, the profound grief of orphaned chimps, playful joy, spontaneous acts of compassion, and enduring social ties.
  • Changing how we refer to animals: She also named the chimpanzees and talked about their unique personalities, which, at the time, was taboo for most scientists. This had a lifelong influence on Marc's research.
  • Documenting unique complex cultural traditions, patterns of social communication, and social relationships: Goodall demonstrated that primates possess distinct regional customs, complex non-verbal communication, and intricate social dynamics, including calculated diplomacy, coalition building, and strategic warfare.
  • Suggesting that chimpanzees performing what she called "waterfall dances" are experiencing wonder and awe.

From discovery to ethical obligation: Using what we know on behalf of other animals

For Goodall, scientific discovery was never an isolated end in itself—it was an invitation to apply that knowledge to improve the welfare of the other sentient beings with whom we share the earth.

Following a 1986 conference in Chicago where she saw covert footage of research chimpanzees in barren steel cages showing signs of severe psychological distress, Jane transitioned from field researcher to full-time advocate.

She campaigned tirelessly to end invasive medical testing on chimps, serving as a key voice in the advocacy coalition that secured passage of the U.S. CHIMP Act to retire laboratory primates to sanctuaries. In 2015, her persistent advocacy contributed to a historic ruling that eliminated the regulatory loophole classifying captive chimps as merely "threatened" and secured full legal protection for them under the Endangered Species Act.

Through works like Harvest for Hope: A Guide to Mindful Eating, her ethical scope reached far beyond primates to challenge factory farming by affirming that farmed animals possess an equal capacity for fear, affection, and family.

In late December 2023, a small group of Jane’s close friends celebrated giving her the secret 90th birthday book and also the coming new year. We did so because we wanted to be sure the book would be a surprise, which it was. Upper row from left to right Mary Lewis (VP - Office of the Founder, The Jane Goodall Institute); Dr. Koen Margodt (co chair of the Ethics Committee of The Jane Goodall Institute); Marc; Lower left: Thomas D. Mangelsen (world-renowned Images of Nature photographer) and Dr. Jane.
Source: Marc Bekoff.

The Power of "Jane Magic"

Goodall recognized that all living beings share an inextricably linked fate—that what we do to the natural world, to animals, we ultimately do to ourselves. Human and non-human animals share a single tapestry of life—and every individual within it holds an intrinsic right to exist free from harm. Her vision helped inspire the principles of compassionate conservation—a holistic ethic uniting human progress, animal well-being, and planetary health. She and Marc argued that conservation goals must never treat individual animals as disposable objects. A firm, quiet, and lighthearted warmth anchored her global influence.

Jane’s contributions are immeasurable. Having worked very closely with her for close to 30 years, I (Marc) don’t think a day went by where I didn’t learn something from her, sometimes directly, sometimes indirectly, often tangible, often intangible. When we were together or talking over Zoom, we would toast one another because we shared a great liking for peaty single malt scotch, which she called her “cough medicine.” Jane was a first-rate scientist, a careful reader and micro-editor, a superb and engaging storyteller, an indefatigable humanitarian, and she had a heart of gold.

Marc and Jane toasting with some "cough medicine."
Source: Thomas D. Mangelsen/Images of Nature.

Jane was a bottomless well; she sent out messages of peace and hope. I feel blessed to have had countless conversations with her in person, on the phone, and over Zoom, and to have travelled with her to discuss science and share stories and jokes. She had a wonderful sense of humor and often complained that people didn’t realize that she had that light side.

I miss Jane every day, but I still talk with her, sometimes to ask her opinion on things, sometimes to say hello and tell her a joke. All in all, Dr. Jane, as many people referred to her, may be one of a kind. I will do all I can to keep "Jane Magic" alive forever.

The Science of Empathy, Kindness, and Sentience

What Jane Goodall understood and demonstrated is that empathy and kindness are not the enemies of scientific rigor. Recognizing that another living being is sentient, has feelings, and a distinct worldview clears our vision rather than clouds it.

Source: Bala Kids/with permission.

She also declared, “Every individual matters. Every individual has a role to play. Every individual makes a difference.”

A year after her passing, her radiance and mission endure. Perhaps the greatest tribute we can offer here is simple: Always treat every single living being with the compassion and reverence they deserve.

Carolyn Cott is the founder and writer of The Kind Life.

item.title: Why Feeling Guilty Doesn't Make You a Better Parent
item.description:
Guilt

Why Feeling Guilty Doesn't Make You a Better Parent

Guilt isn't a badge of honor, it inhibits us, here's why.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Parents feel guilty over 20 times each week.
  • Too much guilt can lead to parental burnout.
  • Understanding how to work with guilt can help.
  • Exercising curiosity is one antidote.

If there's one emotion that parents can't seem to escape, it's guilt. This gnawing emotion grips us when we tell our kids "no," prioritize work, or make a simple parenting mistake. One survey found that parents feel guilty, on average, 23 times a week.

While parental guilt is fairly common, it can leave you feeling stuck, resentful, and fatigued. Guilt drives parents to forgo self-care, or to take on more emotional labor when their plates are full.

Since guilt can feel unbearable, it can also unleash a number of "defenses," which are ways we protect ourselves from emotional pain. Examples include self-criticism (I'm the worst mom because I forgot my kid's lunch), blame (why are you always making things hard, when you know how busy I am), and perfectionism. Of course, these are just a few examples; the list is literally endless.

So often parents deal with guilt by taking action. For example, if you feel guilty about leaving your child with a sitter, you may cancel date night; or if you feel guilty about setting a limit, you may backtrack on the boundary.

Taking action when we don't understand our emotions is like trying to silence a smoke alarm without looking for the fire. It quiets the noise, but it doesn't solve the problem. One of the best ways to navigate parental guilt is to understand the emotion and work through it with emotional wisdom.

What's the purpose of guilt?

In the world of emotions, guilt is called an "inhibitory emotion" because it inhibits other core emotions, such as anger, fear, and sadness. Inhibitory emotions prompt us to follow rules and fit in with society. Guilt nudges us to apologize when we've hurt a friend or lost our cool. In other words, guilt helps us take responsibility for our true wrongdoings.

Parents, however, often feel guilty when they haven't done anything wrong; they just feel like they have. One of the best ways to handle this type of guilt is to ask yourself: "Have I truly done something wrong, or do I just feel like I have?" Chances are, you have not done anything truly egregious (keep in mind that a child's upset isn't necessarily proof that we've made a true mistake).

Calm the body

Emotions don't merely live in our heads; they reside in the body. For example, have you ever noticed how anxiety makes your heart race, or the way sadness makes your heart heavy? Take a moment and think about the last time you felt guilty. Now, what do you notice in your body? Maybe it's a sinking feeling, or your chest feels like it's caving in.

You can help calm your body by taking five deep belly breaths, or by inhaling through your nose, holding it for three counts, and exhaling through pursed lips, like you're blowing on hot soup. Breathing brings oxygen to your muscles, which helps slow your nervous system. This helps you feel calmer.

Call out your guilt

Have you ever wondered why parents are advised to teach their kids to "use their words" when it comes to handling big feelings? Naming our emotions (whether we're 2 or 42) calms the amygdala. It's an emotion regulation strategy that's been proven by science.

Simply saying to yourself (or out loud, or to a trusted friend), "I feel guilty," can defuse this emotion's power over you. Knowing how you feel puts you in a fantastic position to be able to do something about it.

article continues after advertisement

Nurture yourself

Guilt doesn't mean you're a good parent or a bad one. And you're not wrong for feeling guilty. Once you notice and name your guilt, extend yourself compassion.

Here are two phrases that might help:

"I feel guilty right now; all parents feel this way sometimes."

"I feel guilty right now, and this emotion is temporary."

Get curious

Every parent feels guilty now and again, but guilt isn't the end of the story; it's the beginning. Often, guilt inhibits those core emotions, such as sadness, anger, and fear. Guilt may be an emotional reflex, inherited during your own childhood, to keep your own sadness or anger at bay, especially if your parents and caregivers weren't equipped to help you validate and work through these emotions.

Exercising a little curiosity can help. See if you can get a 1/2 inch away from your guilt, and ask yourself: "Is there sadness there?" "Is there anger there?" "Is there fear?"

Core emotions come with adaptive actions that help us flourish and thrive. For example, you may feel guilty when you're really angry about something. Once you identify this, you're in a very different position. Anger may mean that you feel violated or that a boundary has been crossed. Sadness means there's something to mourn. For example, a parent may feel guilty for missing back-to-school night or the school field trip. But upon further exploration, sadness may be at the root.

And identifying this (or any other core emotion) is a game-changer, not just for parenting, but also for life.

The next time parental guilt rears its head, follow this recipe for emotional well-being.
