item.title: 'Buddy' the Unicorn and the Terrors of Childhood
item.description:
Fear

'Buddy' the Unicorn and the Terrors of Childhood

A strange horror movie accesses the endurance of childhood fears.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Childhood fears do not always go away when we become adults.
  • The fear of death, which we acquire around the age of 6, never leaves us.
  • The movie "Buddy" reminds us of the magic and horror of our childhood interior lives.

Recently, there have been a number of really interesting horror movies hitting the big screens. One of the most unusual is called "Buddy." It is a strange film about a fluffy orange unicorn on a children’s TV show. Buddy is not our friend. Though he sings and plays with the kids, he is actually a murderous monster who controls a dark dimension.

Obviously a riff on the '90s kids’ show "Barney," "Buddy" opens with what look like actual episodes of a music-oriented kids show, featuring a friendly unicorn, along with pals such as a talking mailbox and a friendly nurse. Soon, however, it becomes apparent that something is very wrong here. Buddy is an evil entity.

While Barney the Dinosaur has been subject to a surprising plethora of dark urban legends and parodies, Buddy is effective because it also taps into the terrors that arise in our childhoods that manage to linger in our subconscious throughout our lives.

How Childhood Fears Persist Into Adulthood

In a Scientific American article, psychologist Ellen Hendriksen notes that childhood fears do not always go away when we become adults. “[S]urprisingly often, childhood fears stick around well into adulthood…maybe your fear has evolved, but fundamentally stayed the same. For example, a childhood fear of monsters may have morphed into a fear of burglars (how many locks are on your door?). A fear of strangers may have turned into social anxiety.”

The fear of death, which we seem to acquire around the age of 6 or so, never leaves us. In fact, studies show that this primal fear rises and falls depending upon our age. Born in our impressionable youth, the fear of death manifests itself in many ways throughout our lives.

Buddy the unicorn brings us back to these worrisome early childhood years. These were the years when we were glued to the TV, watching fantastical characters teach us about being friends, sharing our toys, and obeying safety rules. But these were also years that witnessed the activation of numerous novel fears, such as monsters lurking under the bed, “strangers” in the neighborhood, the sounds of things going bump in the night, and even death itself.

Psychologist Bruce Hood has conjectured that as children, we “infer hidden energies and properties to living things” and even to inanimate objects. The “blankie” that we cannot part with or replace is a classic example of the object imbued with fairylike energy. This magical thinking does not leave us. Even our adult brains are wired to see “hidden structures, patterns, energies, and dimensions to reality.” Our childhood obsessions and fears, even when grounded in nonrational thoughts, live on. They are the shadows sticking to the back of our supposedly rational minds.

This shadowy place is the fountain of fear that Buddy so effectively capitalizes on. There is a scene in the film in which Buddy is torched in flame. He lives, and underneath the fur, we see a gory, hideous interior. His monstrous insides evoke the terrors that emerge in childhood, terrors that we struggle to cope with. Though we loved to watch happy animals tell us that everything was OK, we also were learning on our own that our loved ones may not permanently be with us. On playgrounds, we’d hear of kids disappearing from parks and street corners, never to be seen again. We gradually came to understand that horrible things were happening everywhere.

article continues after advertisement

The dissonance of Barney singing about friendship, in his bright, happy TV world, often jarred against an emergent reality of childhood anxieties and fears. This contradiction never resolves. We learn to cope with the darkness, but we never really conquer it. The fears will morph and live on, in a variety of ways, for many of us.

How "Buddy" Provides Catharsis for Adult Audiences

"Buddy" capitalizes on this moment of contradiction. As adults watching in the theater, we are reminded of the magic and horror of our childhood interior lives. The experience is both frightening and cathartic. Buddy’s evil evokes fear. But it also, strangely, reassures us, letting us know that we were right to feel ever-so-slightly-betrayed by our furry friends on the small screen. This catharsis helps us to cope with the terrors that have never left.

item.title: How to Get AI to Help You With a Task You’re Avoiding
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

How to Get AI to Help You With a Task You’re Avoiding

AI's robotic nature can help us emotionally unload to-dos that feel heavy.

Posted October 5, 2026

Source: AI generated image.

We all have tasks we avoid. They’re to-dos we feel uncomfortable with for some reason.

They might be big or they might be small.

For example, recently, I needed to find a way to courier a document to myself from overseas. I know how to send a document from the US (where I live) to another country, but the reverse route was unfamiliar. I’d had this task on my to-do list for several weeks, and it was lingering in an annoying, slightly draining way.

Tasks we avoid can be those:

  • That we’re doing for the first time
  • That we rarely do
  • That require extreme attention to detail, like not getting numbers wrong
  • That are inherently emotional (like death- or health-related)
  • That we resent having to do
  • That have accumulated mental load from past avoidance
  • That have accumulated mental load for some other reason, e.g., because our past self wasn't as skilled at them as our current self can be, and we’re carrying that

Even if you have no interest in using AI, recognizing the above categories and how they’re linked to your sense of burden can help enough to get you moving on an avoided to-do item.

3 Ways to Use AI to Get Past Avoidance

These strategies can still be used by those who are unimpressed by AI and who would generally like it involved in their life less, not more.

If you’re avoiding a task, and that avoidance is going to continue otherwise, you have very little to lose by trying these.

1. One-Shot It to Observe AI’s Initial Actions

One-shotting is when you give an AI a prompt and let it do a task its own way. If you’re fussy and picky (as I am), that will rarely be good enough for you. But it’s a wonderful strategy for curious observation of exactly what the AI does without you having to think about how you would do the task first.

For example, for sending my documents, I did a quick Reddit search that suggested only one courier company was as reliable as I needed for the specific overseas country involved. I then said to the AI, “Find me the best rate for sending a 10-page document from NZ to the US in under three days using [company]. I don’t want to pay rack rates.” Not quite one-shotting (since I did the Reddit search), but close. I used Claude in Chrome so it could control my browser and actually fill in dropdowns to get quotes.

2. Nudge the Task Along and Let It Breathe

After I gave the AI the instruction, I left it and didn’t even look back at the conversation for a few hours. I checked back and saw it had done a pretty good job.

It wasn’t until a few days later, when I had the mental energy for finalizing everything, that I followed up, went back and forth with it a few times, and eventually had it write a paragraph of instructions I could paste into a message for my shipper.

(Since this lack of urgency is probably confusing, let me clarify: The document needed to arrive quickly after it was finalized, but it wasn't actually finalized and ready to send when I was doing my initial searches.)

This is a strategy I have named “nudge and breathe” for myself. It means to nudge a task forward as my mental energy allows. Since the AI acts as if no time has passed, this works well. It takes a lot of pressure off. It’s like handing a ball back and forth between you and the AI, but letting the ball just sit in the AI’s hands for hours, days, or even weeks or months.

3. Quick Tests When You Expect Getting to Exactly What You Want Will Be Hard

This week, I had a situation where I wanted to print some additional numbers into a document after it had been signed by someone else. (Not as dodgy as it sounds, I promise.) I wasn’t sure if this would work, and I didn’t want to handwrite numbers into tiny fields unless I had to.

Initially, AI had given me a bunch of unsatisfying answers about whether this could be done reliably (since I couldn’t mess up the signed page).

Eventually I said, “Let’s just test it.” It created a test in one minute, and in fact showed that all its worries about potential paper shifts and everything else the AI mentioned could go wrong did not match reality.

Without AI, me figuring out how to test this would’ve taken a long time. Together, the AI and I did it in under 10 minutes and saved me the stress of relying on my anything-but-neat handwriting.

The Same Strategies Work for More Substantial Avoided Tasks

I illustrated the techniques here with mundane (but heavy to me) examples, but that’s only because those are more easily described in a blog post. The same strategies work for breaking down bigger and more important avoidances too. The beauty of AI for this type of work is that it doesn’t think like you. It can be robotic when you’re anxious, resentful, depleted, or whatever state is underlying your avoidance.

Looping an AI into a task can emotionally unload it for us. This can be valuable even for those who have no interest in optimization or hyper-productivity.

item.title: What You Really Need to Be More Attractive
item.description:
Beauty

What You Really Need to Be More Attractive

Consumer culture says beauty is in the makeup aisle. Science tells us otherwise.

Posted October 5, 2026

Key points
  • Beauty products promise us smoother skin and bigger eyes, but attraction runs far deeper than looks.
  • Attraction begins before we ever say a word: a relaxed, unhurried presence is what really draws people in.
  • In conversation, it’s kindness and responsiveness that make us more attractive.
  • Consumer culture hurries us away from ease and kindness, but a few simple practices can bring us back.
Source: iStockphoto/LUMEZIA

It happens to all of us now and then, and it happened to me just a few days ago while strolling through Ljubljana, Slovenia, dressed in my casual American attire and passing a long line of people whose style seemed impeccable. Suddenly, I felt it: Unattractive. The next morning, things got worse: I awoke to find a shiny red pimple had sprouted overnight on the left side of my nose. (How does that even happen?)

It doesn’t take much for us to start doubting our looks because everywhere we turn—TikTok, Instagram, billboards—we see people with smooth skin, big eyes, small noses, slim frames, and the whispered (sometimes shouted) message is, You should look like them. Then comes consumer culture’s promise: And you can, if you buy__. It’s billions of dollars riding on us believing that it’s all just one small purchase away.

But page after page of research on attraction tells us things consumer culture would rather we never knew because what consumer culture can do is sell us products promising smoother skin, brighter eyes, smaller noses, slimmer frames, and it can convince us that the latest bottle will finally close the gap between our face and the one on the packaging; but what consumer culture can’t do is bottle and sell what science tells us about true attractiveness.

Let’s get this out of the way first. Do the Hollywood good looks these products promote matter? Yes, they do, but far less than consumer culture would have us believe. At first blush, we tend to find faces attractive when they’re symmetrical rather than unusual (with no pimple on the left side of their nose) (Little and colleagues, 2007; Rhodes, 2006). But pouring our energy into winning at this surface game is a poor investment because more lasting measures of attractiveness lie elsewhere (Hunt and colleagues, 2015; Kononov and Ein-Gar, 2025).

No Store Can Sell It

Attraction begins before we ever say a word, not in the simple way consumer culture suggests (the beautiful woman in the red dress or the handsome man in the black tux pulling us inescapably toward them by the sheer force of their facial symmetry). Instead, picture that woman in red (or the man in black) coming toward us from down the street, stunning at first blush, but as they draw closer we sense they’re tense, rushing, irritable, even braced for conflict. Our bodies pick up on all of these signals, nervous system to nervous system; we tense up too, and in no time the attraction fades.

Now flip the script and imagine someone new walking toward us, an everyday woman in a plain sweatshirt (or everyday man in Levi’s), but this time, in their gait and facial expression, we sense something completely different: a relaxed, unhurried ease. Again, our physiology tunes in to what they’re transmitting, and we find ourselves drawn to them, sometimes surprisingly so. Below conscious awareness, we tune into each other’s nervous systems; whenever someone’s presence creates a shared ease, a positivity resonance, there’s a magnetic, energetic sense of bonding (Prochazkova and colleagues, 2022; Wells and colleagues, 2022).

We won’t find “open, relaxed presence” in the beauty aisles of our local grocer, because consumer culture can’t bottle that one up. Worse, consumer culture pushes us toward its opposite: it insists there’s always something more to do, somewhere else to be, something more to buy; it rushes us about, and soon our nervous systems are broadcasting “out-of-sorts” to the very people we hope will find us attractive. If we want to draw people to us, we have to find a different approach. But wait, there’s more.

A Sad Irony

After the approach comes the conversation, and how we converse quickly shapes how much people like us, how close they feel to us (Huang and colleagues, 2017), and, yes, how physically attractive they find us (Kononov and Ein-Gar, 2025; Niimi and Goto, 2023). The lever for raising all three is kindness and responsiveness, propositions that sound easy enough. But demonstrating kindness and being responsive require a willingness to make real time for people and to genuinely engage with them (no glancing at our watches, no wishing we were somewhere else), and in a consumer culture determined to hurry us, that’s no small task.

I’m reminded of the story of the Good Samaritan, though I’ve come to understand it a little differently. A man lies beaten on the side of the road; a priest and a Levite pass him by without stopping; then a Samaritan comes along, kneels, tends to the man’s wounds, and carries him to safety. I’ve often wondered: Why didn’t the priest and Levite help? And I’ve come to think it wasn’t because they were bad people, but because they were hurried. They had robes to press, sermons to deliver, and no time to stop; but the Samaritan, by contrast, took his time (Darley and Batson, 1973).

There’s a sad irony here, consumer culture promising to make us beautiful one bottle at a time, all the while hurrying us away from the very kindness and responsiveness that science tells us make us genuinely attractive.

If the science points us somewhere the beauty aisle can’t take us, how do we get there? It takes only a few simple, human-sized practices—ones we can easily weave into everyday life.

A Human-Sized Practice

As we approach someone new, we call in stillness (the art of greeting each moment with curiosity instead of demand) by slowing down, taking a few deep breaths, and letting our nervous system settle. Then we summon compassion (the art of keeping our heart open to ourselves and one another, come what may) by silently repeating a few words from the loving-kindness meditation: May we all be safe. May we all be free. May we all be at peace, a little softer, gentler, slower with each repetition.

Our body relaxes, our stance opens, and when we sit down to talk, we find ourselves listening and lounging with others, all the things that make us attractive, no purchase necessary. If only I’d remembered this in Europe, pimple and all.
